subtopic: COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY AND WAYS AND MEANS BEFORE ADDRESS AGREED TO

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY AND WAYS AND MEANS BEFORE ADDRESS AGREED TO
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called I desire to raise a point of order. It is in reference to the construction to be placed upon standing order No. 57 of this house. The order is as follows:
The house shall appoint the committees of supply, and ways and means, at the commencement of every session, so soon as an address has been agreed to in answer to His Excellency's speech.
On Friday evening last the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) gave what he stated was the government's interpretation of the meaning of that order, which was to the effect that the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means must be appointed immediately after the conclusion of the debate on the address, but that there was nothing in the order which precluded the committees being set up before the address had been agreed to. The Prime Minister was careful to say that he would not say that the contention of the government was right, and you, Mr. Speaker, have not as yet been asked to rule on the matter. I am bringing up the matter at this moment, not for the purpose of in any way delaying procedure or of embarrassing the government, but rather to avoid both those possibilities. I have thought it better to raise the question before the government itself makes any formal motion to go into supply.
Last might the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) who was the acting leader of the house, mentioned that it was the intention of the government to move to go into supply to-day. I have thought it advisable, in order that the matter may be discussed in a wholly dispassionate manner, as a matter of procedure which really concerns members on all sides of the house, and in no sense a party issue to raise the question in the form in which I am raising it at the moment.
It is obvious, from the reading of the rule of this house, that it is copied literatim et verbatim from the rule of the House of Commons at Westminster. There are two words which appear in the order at Westminster that do not appear in our order, the words "in future," but they in no way affect its purpose. The order of the British house is standing order No. 14, it reads as follows:
This house will, in future, appoint the committees of supply and ways and means at the commencement of every session, so soon as an address has been agreed to, in answer to His Majesty's speech.
The interpretation to be placed upon the order by the British house is best given by the leading constitutional authorities on procedure in the commons, and on the law and custom of the constitution. I shall therefore quote from three or four of the most eminent authorities. It will be apparent, once the quotations are given, that there is no longer room for doubt as to what the intention of the order is.
288	COMMONS
Business of the House-Procedure
May's Parliamentary Practice at page 520 of the 13th edition, published in 1924, has the following:
The action taken by the House of Commons upon the demand of aid and supply for the public service made by the speech from the throne, is the appointment, pursuant to standing order No. 14, of those committees of the whole house, which are known as the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means. Motions setting up these committees are made immediately after the house agrees to the address in answer to the speech from the throne, and are put forthwith from the chair, no debate being permitted thereon.
Hon. members will observe that the wording is not that they " may be " or " must be '' established but that they " are " established immediately after the house agrees to the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Anson's Law of the Constitution, volume I, fifth edition, 1922, page 286, states:
The speech from the throne always contains a demand from the crown for supply, and as soon as the House of Commons has agreed upon an address in reply to the speech, it has for many years passed two resolutions-one that on a certain day it will resolve itself into committee of supply; another that on a certain day it will resolve itself into committee of ways and means.
Here we have a positive statement of the customary method of procedure. I submit it is custom that governs in matters of this kind.
I refer next to Redlich's Procedure of the House of Commons, 1907, volume 3, page 133:
In response to the speech from the throne the commons, as soon as they have voted the address in reply, appoint the two great committees before which the whole finance of the year has to be discussed-the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means.
That is very specific language; as soon as they have voted the address in reply they appoint the committees. It is, I think, conclusive in its wording and meaning.
One further authority I should like to quote is Campion. In his Introduction to the Procedure of the House of Commons, first edition, 1929, page 235, this writer says:
The committee of supply is " set up " immediately after the conclusion of the debate on the address in answer to the king's speech by resolution in the following form:
Resolved, that this house will, to-morrow, resolve itself into a committee to consider of the supply to be granted to His Majesty."
The committee of ways and means is similarly set up at the same time.
The authorities I have quoted Mr. Speaker, are authorities we are continually quoting in this house, and are recognized as eminent authorities. I admit at once there

have been occasions in the British house when other matters have been taken up before the debate on the address was concluded, but always where such has been the case they have been in the nature of exceptions; they have been matters of some special significance at the moment, questions which for some special reason required to be dealt with at the time they were, and as to which the results might have been unfortunate had there been delay. What I am afraid of is that in this house we may be changing a custom by the exceptions we are making, that the government is not viewing the proposed course so much as an exception as it is seeking to make what has been an exception in the last session or two a custom which will govern in the future.
This matter is of importance, not only does it affect this house at this session, but the decision that will be given by His Honour the Speaker undoubtedly will be cited with reference to procedure in future years. Undoubtedly the rules are amongst other things for the purpose of protecting the rights of lion, members of the house.
With regard to the interpretation put upon the order by the Prime Minister, I submit that there is no necessity for a rule at all to ensure what the Prime Minister has said is the purpose to be served. The government is all powerful; its rights do not need to be secured by a special rule as to the time within which committees must be appointed. Except where there is a rule to the contrary, it has the pow'er to select its own time. But the minority in the house has in many particulars to be protected in its rights, especially at a time when for obvious reasons the government is finding it more and more necessary to take to itself as much right of way as may be possible for the prosecution of public business. The fact that the government is taking more and more of the time of the house for the government's own program, makes it more necessary for the opposition, regardless of what party may be in opposition, to see that the few rights that remain to hon. members to discuss generally the questions that are of great concern to them are preserved as far as may be possible. The interpretation that is being put upon this rule, especially when considered in relation to what is now being proposed, namely, that before the debate on the address is concluded, the house should resolve itself into a committee of supply to appropriate public moneys, makes the matter one which I think should be settled immediately and that in accordance with what I have shown to be

Business oj the House-Procedure
the prevailing custom in the British House of Commons.
The point I wish to make is this, that even if we admit for a moment that the rule is to be interpreted so as to give the government the right to set up these committees immediately, it does not necessarily follow that because the committees are set up, the house should proceed to go into committee of supply or committee of ways and means before the debate on the address is concluded. Indeed Redlich, whom the Prime Minister cites frequently as an authority, is quite positive in his statement on that point. Volume I, page 41, of Redlich's Procedure of the House of Commons, contains the following:
It is already a fixed custom that the Queen's speech is to be answered by an address which takes the first place in the deliberations of the house.
That is the point I desire to stress particularly at the moment. I believe it was to ensure that the address would take first place in the deliberations of the house that rule 20 was enacted, and where the rule is followed as interpreted by the authorities I have quoted it is pretty obvious that the debate on the address will take first place in our deliberations.
To show how important it is that the customary practice should be maintained may I direct attention to what would happen in the natural order of things if the opposition were considering a motion of want of confidence in the government on going into supply, and there was no other motion before the house. The opposition might wish to move that the motion to go into supply be amended by striking out all the words after the word "that" in the customary motion and substituting therefor the words "the government does not enjoy the confidence of the house." That might delay indefinitely both supply and the completion of the debate on the address. That would be a very natural motion to make at any time of going into supply. But assume that such an amendment were to be moved this afternoon to a motion that the house resolve itself into committee of supply, what would be our position? Already there is before the house a motion to the effect that the address should be amended by directing the attention of His Excellency to the fact that the government does not enjoy the confidence of the country. It is quite true that that amendment though it refers to the country is similar in meaning to the amendment I have suggested which -would refer to the house. Both are in the nature of want of confidence motions. I submit that before the debate on the want of confidence motion 74726-19
now before us is concluded, we should not run the risk of entering upon another debate which would certainly arise out of a want of confidence amendment being moved to any motion by the government to resolve the house into a committee of supply. I think, I have only to cite this possibility to make perfectly clear how obvious it is that rule 20 was intended to ensure the completion of the debate on the address before the house should go on with the discussion of any other question.
Of course there is the further fact that the first few days of the session are supposed to be devoted as well to getting the routine business under way and the machinery of business properly established. It always has been the practice, while the debate on the address was proceeding, to have different committees named, to have bills introduced, and to deal with other matters of routine, but not to proceed in discussion with matters of a substantial character until the debate on the address was concluded. May I ask if it is not something more than an anomally for the Commons to be asked to vote supply to His Majesty so long as there remains before the house as an order of business and of current discussion the question as to whether or not the government enjoys the confidence of the house or of the country?
Having submitted the matter in this form, I hope the Prime Minister will not to-day press his motion for going into supply, when the item is reached upon the orders of the day, but will allow the matter if need be to be further carefully considered between members of all parties in the house, so that the best procedure may be followed and the rights of all hon. members protected not only at this session but for subsequent sessions as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a word in reply to some of the observations of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). In the first place, if he will read the rule which applies to this House of Commons, known as standing order 57, he will find the following:
The house shall appoint the committee of supply and ways and means at the commencement of every session, so soon as an address has been agreed to, in answer to His Excellency's speech.
That, I assume, means that there is a limitation in regard to the time in which we shall appoint these committees. We shall not delay appointment of these important committees. The conclusion of the address in reply to His Excellency's speech Shall be the



Business oj the House-Procedure
limit of tame for the house to appoint these committees. There is no rule of the house, so far as I know, which precludes an earlier appointment of these committees, if the house sees fit to do so. We are all aware that upon 'he opening day of each session of this House of Commons, for the express purpose of preserving the right of parliament to deal with other subjects prior to our consideration of the address of His Excellency, a formal bill is introduced respecting oaths of office. There is no reason for the introduction of such a bill apart from the single purpose of preserving the right of parliament to deal with such other business 'as it may see fit before taking into consideration the speech of His Excellency the Governor General.
I submit that any business can 'be taken up. Conditions may arise which render it very necessary to discuss some emergent condition, buit there is no limitation to the right of the house to deal with any subject. Any business which might later come before the House of Commons can be taken up in priority to the speech from the throne if the house so determines. The citation from Redlieh cited by the leader of the opposition is merely to the effect that the address in reply to His Excellency's speech shall be the first order of proceedings. At the opening of this session we did constitute it the very first order, and there it remains upon the order paper. In this practice we are following the course which is invariably adopted in England. After the mover and seconder have made their speeches and, as a rule, after the leaders of the various parties have replied, very often there occurs an adjournment of the debate and other business is permitted to intervene.
May, which I have had an opportunity of examining only for a moment sets out at page 173:
When the royal speech lias been read, an address in answer thereto is moved in both houses. Two members in each house are selected by the administration for moving and seconding the address and they appear in their places in levee dress for that purpose. The form of the address used to be an answer, paragraph by paragraph, to the speech. In both lords and commons since the commencement of session 1890-91, the answer to the royal speech has been moved in the form of a single resolution, expressing their thanks to the Sovereign for the most gracious speech addressed to both houses of parliament, and amendments to the address are moved by way of addition thereto. The transaction of public business is carried on whilst the proceedings on the address are in progress, bills being introduced and committees appointed. In session 1884, debate on the address was postponed from day to day, whilst a motion of censure on the government, regarding events in the Soudan, was under consideration, and in session 1922 whilst two bills pre-

sented by the government together with the financial resolution necessary for one of them were passed through all their stages.
There is no limitation expressed by May as to the nature of business which may be taken up. It is important for the prompt dispatch of business in this house that the committees in question should be established as early as possible; it is important to facilitate the transaction of business that the estimates be opened on a Tuesday, because we know that under the rules of the house unless the various departments are first discussed on a Tuesday they cannot subsequently be taken up on a Thursday or Friday. So that for the prompt dispatch of business in the house the present motion is very necessary. The motion that the house go into committee of supply on this Tuesday will enable us to discuss supply on Thursday and Friday. Unless there is a positive prohibition in some rule of this house or an established custom in the British House of Commons binding upon this house I submit we are at liberty to take up any item of business which the house may deem proper, pending our subsequent consideration of the speech of His Excellency. Therefore I take it that the point of order is not well taken, and that the house is at liberty to proceed at this time with business as it sees fit.
I do not quite agree with my right hon. friend in the statement he has first made concerning the rules of parliament. He has stated that the rules are for the purpose of protecting the rights of hon. members in the house. That may be one effect of them, but my submission is that the rules are expressly framed to facilitate public business in this chamber, and to achieve this purpose, the rules should not receive a narrow or limited construction. Rule 57, as now framed, is in its effect a mandatoiy order upon the House of Commons not to delay the setting up of the committees of ways and means and of supply later than the conclusion of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. But there is nothing of a prohibitory nature in this rule. There is no limitation as to what business shall be taken up or what shall not be taken up, and we know that by immemorial usage we are at liberty to take up such business as the house deems proper.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I submit that the motion to go into supply at this stage should not be entertained. Indeed, to move such a motion at the present time is, in my view, treating the house with scant courtesy. I do not agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) as to the manner in which the debate
29r

Business oj the House-Procedure
on the address should be conducted and has been conducted in this House of Commons and in the British parliament. The debate in question is one of the two important debates of the session. Members of parliament after a long adjournment come from their respective constituencies and have a right to say what public opinion is in their respective sections of the country. They have the right to present to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house the views on various public questions of the people they represent, and it has always been the custom and practice to let this debate go on before taking up other public matters.
First I shall quote from Bourinot, Fourth edition, page 95 as to the practice in Canada:
It is not usual in the Canadian houses to discuss any important matter of public policy before considering the speech. In 1901, an address was passed to His Majesty King Edward, expressive of the national grief on the demise of Queen Victoria, and of the continued attachment of the dominion to His Majesty's person and government, before the address in answer to the speech was taken up. In 1878, Mr. Barthe introduced a bill in reference to insolvency, but withdrew it in deference to the wishes of the house until the address was adopted. While bills are formally introduced and advanced a stage, the house generally consents to postpone notices of motion until after the disposal of the address. Of course, the public interests may at some time demand that the house should act otherwise, and-as it is undoubtedly its constitutional right-take up immediately a question of public importance and deal with it. It is usual in the British commons to ask questions, move addresses or orders for papers, present petitions and introduce as well as discuss public bills before the address has been adopted. In the session of 1884 " debate on the address was adjourned from day to day while a motion of censure on the government regarding ' events in the Soudan ' was under consideration."
But that was an exception, and at the bottom of the page, 96, Bourinot says:
In 1889 Mr. Abbott introduced in the Senate three government bills mentioned in the speech, before the address in answer thereto was considered. Objection was taken to this departure from the ordinary course of procedure. The bills were placed on the order paper for consideration subsequent to the address. In the following session the usual procedure was resumed.
If hon. gentlemen will look at the following pages, 98, and 99, they will see t'he interpretation that Bourinot gives to rule 57 as to the appointment of the committee of supply. After referring to the adoption of the address he says:
The next proceeding will be to move immediately that the house resolve itself at some future day into committees of supply and of ways and means. It is also usual to move at this stage of the proceedings the appointment of a chairman of committees when such appoint-74726-I9J
ment has to be made at the beginning of a new parliament or in the case of a vacancy in such office.
The same thing is done in the British House of Commons. I shall quote briefly from Todd's Parliamentary Government in England, Volume 2, page 366. He says:
Pending the agreement of the house to the address questions may be put to ministers, and addresses passed for the production of papers.
You see how it is limited. It goes on:
But it is usual to defer the presentation of papers asked for and to postpone a formal reply to an ordinary address, until the answer of the crown to this address has been reported.
Last year the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said that he did not want to follow the practice in this house but wanted to adopt the British practice. Nobody said a word. I thought that possibly during the last few years a new practice had been introduced in the British House of Commons, but I took the trouble this morning to go to the parliamentary library and look into the debates of the British House of Commons.
In 1928 the address was moved on November 6 and was immediately taken up, debated again on November 7, November 8 and November 9, and then it was adjourned from Friday the 9bh to Monday the 12th, When it was again taken up, and again on November 13, again on November 14 and concluded on that day-seven days altogether.
I also found that a number of members varying from ten to fifteen spoke during the debate each day. As hon. gentlemen know, there is no eleven o'clock rule in the British House of Commons, and a considerable number of members speak during those debates.
In 1929 the address started on July 2, was taken up again on July 3, July 4, July 5, adjourned from Friday to Monday, July 8, when it was again taken up, again on July 9 and July 10, when it was concluded.
In 1930 the address was moved and discussed on October 28, taken up again on October 29, October 30, October 31, adjourned from Friday to Monday, November 3, taken up on that day and again on November 4, when it was concluded.
In 1931 the address was moved and discussed on November 10, taken up again on November 11, November 12, November 13, adjourned from Friday to Monday, and concluded on that day.
In 1932 the address was moved on November 22, discussed again on November 23, November 24, November 25, adjourned from Friday to Monday, November 28, and disposed, of on that day.

Business oj the House-Procedure
In the present session, 1933, there was an exception for one day. The address was moved and discussed on November 21, and then it was decided that on the following day the house would discuss constitutional reform in India, which was a burning question which the house wanted to discuss immediately, but that occupied only one day and the address was taken up again on November 23, November 24, adjourned from Friday to Monday, November 27, taken up again on that day, and again on November 28, when it was disposed of.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if it were not for the somewhat rhetorical observations which the hon. gentleman who has just taken his place (Mr. Lapointe) made at the close of his remarks, it would perhaps not be necessary to rise at all. The rules of this house are made by the house and no one else. They are prepared by a committee of the house and submitted to the house for its approval. Therefore, they are not the rules of a government or an opposition, they are the rules that the members comprising parliament have thought desirable to enact. For what purpose? For the purpose of governing their proceedings; not for minorities or majorities, but for the orderly conduct of the business of the House of Commons. That is what the rules are for. It must be remembered that the miles of this house are not identical with the rules of the British House of Commons. They differ in many particulars. I shall point out presently one particular in which they differ and which has brought about the present discussion.

Business of the House-Procedure
It will be recalled that at the first session at which this government assumed office we were desirous of expediting the business of the House of Commons. I suggested to the leader of the opposition that we should proceed with the address on Friday but he thought it undesirable that we should depart from the practice or custom. Therefore, we waited until Monday when the mover and seconder of the address made their speeches. In Great Britain this is not the rule. I shall take last year as an example. The British House of Commons was opened on November 21, 1933, as reported in the fifth series, volume 283. The house met at twelve of the clock, Mr. Speaker in the chair. The sessional orders were then debated, some questions were asked with respect to certain matters, written answers were given and then the King's speech was proceeded with, as reported on page seven. The Speaker indicated that a copy of the speech had been obtained and the debate on the address proceeded. The King had delivered his speech that day. Mr. Cross moved the motion that afternoon and concluded his speech, as did the seconder of the motion. Sir Herbert Samuel and the leader of the government, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, concluded their speeches and the debate was continued into the evening. The motion to adjourn the debate was made by Mr. Edwards, and it was agreed that the debate should be adjourned until the morrow. Then followed the motion, "that this house do now adjourn," and the house was adjourned at twenty-one minutes before eight o'clock on the day upon which the King had delivered his speech. We do not do business here quite so expeditiously. The leaders of the parties and the mover and seconder of the address do not dispose of their speeches by twenty-one minutes before eight o'clock of the day upon which the speech from the throne is delivered. But on succeeding days the question as to when the debate shall be resumed is determined in one of two ways. If no motion is made that it shall have precedence, it takes its place upon the order paper under the appropriate heading.
In days gone by it has been the custom in this chamber to give precedence to this debate. The right hon. gentleman when in power used to move a motion, as will be seen in the journals of the house, that the debate do have precedence and thereupon it had precedence over all other business and was proceeded with until it was ended. I intimated last year-this is where my friend the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) apparently has misunderstood-that it would take its place upon the order paper under the appropriate heading. This was done last year, the year before and in 1930. It was also done this year when the leader of the opposition asked me whether or not I was going to ask this chamber, which has control of its own proceedings, to give precedence to the debate or leave it to take its place upon the order paper. I told him I proposed to leave it to take its place upon the order paper in accordance with the rules of the house. In other words, I declined to depart from the rules and to-day the address in reply to the speech from the throne occupies a place upon the order paper which is its appropriate 'place according to the rules. The right hon. gentleman was quite right in asking me whether I proposed to ask the house to change the rules, but I said no, that I proposed to leave the rules to their operation, just as they do in England. Every day this house has been in session, if other business had been disposed of it could have taken up the debate on the speech from the throne when it was reached under its appropriate heading.
I did not change the order of business. Why should we? What are rules for? Why does the right hon. gentleman want us to change the rules? Why does the former Minister of Justice ask that this house should change its rules? We have left the rules as they are and have declined to alter them and give precedence to this debate. The hon. gentlemen who formulated these rules did not so provide and only this House of Commons by motion made can change the rules covering the hearing of this debate. If it so desires, this house can say that this debate shall have precedence over all other business and if it has precedence over all other business, it has precedence over this business because this chamber, like any deliberative assembly, has said that we shall now go on with this business first and take something else second. But there is an absence of any such motion. I presented no such motion; I said: We do not intend to do so. That being so, it just goes on in the even tenor of its way as it does in England, taking its place under the appropriate heading and being called when other matters have been disposed of. The business of the house proceeds in the orderly fashion which parliament has fixed.
I ask this chamber and I ask every hon. member of at who wants to be fair: Why all this discussion when we have done nothing but cling to the rules which were made? The complaint is that we have not departed from them and that I have not moved to give this matter precedence. But I followed the English custom. I have in my hand the opening Hansards for the last four years. When the

Business of the House-Procedure
former Minister of Justice said that this debate had taken precedence he surely could not have read these as carefully as he usually does. The fact is that this debate did not take precedence. It took its place under the appropriate heading.	_
Now, all you have to do is to turn to the records of the British House of Commons for November 23, 1932, which was the day after the house had opened. The house met at a quarter to three in the afternoon, Mr. Speaker in the chair, and we find this order of business: Private legislation; Procedure (Scotland) Act of 1899, Sir George Collins; Expiring Laws Continuance Bill, one of the most important bills, moved by Mr. Hore-Belisha, one of the Under-Secretaries, Bill No. 1; Mr. Speaker ordered that the ballot should take place in Room No. 10; business of the house; amendments on going into committee of supply.
There is a motion passed before the debate was considered, that no notices of amendments on going into committee of supply be given until the first Thursday after the adjournment of the House of Commons.
Then we find: The Prime Minister, London Passenger Transport Bill, perhaps the most important of all public bills that have to be considered; ordered, that the proceedings of the London Passenger Transport Bill be resumed-Bill No. 2, fixed for Monday next.

Then we come to the next day, the 24th. What happened on the 24th? We find: Questions, just as we have them here, the proper order of business; the debate stood where it was. Then followed, on the 28th day of November, the house having adjourned over the weekend, something which I desire to point out as being of very considerable importance. Questions were on the order paper-Private Business, Oral Answers to Questions.- Then followed certain questions oral and written, and then the King's speech and the resumption of the address with respect thereto. That is that year. But I will point out in one moment that in another year something far more important took place. Mr. Baldwin, as Lord President of the Privy Council, moved a motion which involved a very serious debate in which a division was taken resulting in the government being sustained in the views it put forth. I think it important to turn that up in order that the house may have the record complete, and to show that what we have done has been to follow the course exactly as laid down in the British House of Commons.
You will find, for example, in 1931, certain bills introduced, including as a matter of fact the Westminster Act-introduced by the Secretary of State for the Dominions while the debate was pending. Under bills presented we find the Educational Endowments (Scotland) Bill, and then questions with regard to the Royal Navy (Discharges), National Savings Certificates, and matters of that character.

speechtext:
Perhaps the hon, gentleman will wait until I have reached that. I want to demolish one thing at a time; I have now demolished entirely the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite, but I desire to point out one other matter, namely, a motion made by Mr. Baldwin prior to the house continuing the debate; I wish to show the division that took place with respect thereto before the debate was continued. At page 105 of the debates for 1931 we find, while the debate was still pending, that Bill No. 5, the Indian Pay (Temporary Abatements) Bill was introduced on that day before the debate was continued; and under private business we find a bill with respect to Edinburgh Corporation; the Kilmarnock Gas Provisional Order Bill, which was disposed of, and afterwards Mr. Baldwin, Lord President of the Council, rose in his place and moved:
That until the adjournment of the house for Christmas, government business do have precedence at every sitting, that no bills other than government bills be introduced, tmd that no ballot be taken for determining the precedence of such bills.
That brought about a discussion in which Mr. Lansbury stated his view; Mr. Tinker spoke; Lieutenant-Colonel Moore, Mr. Max-ton, and others. The house divided, the ayes being 378 and the noes 9. At page 148 we find a further motion was made by Mr. Baldwin:
That no notice of amendment on going into committee of supply be given until after the adjournment of the house for Christmas.
That was carried without division. We find on page 119 that the debate was resumed, Mr. Gwilym Lloyd George having made certain proposals with respect to it.
Now that proves conclusively that we are following the course that has been followed in the British House of Commons, namely, taking up the debate in reply to the speech from the throne when it has been reached under its appropriate heading, not before and not after; because we have declined to make a motion to give it precedence over every other business. In other words, it takes its place on the order paper. That disposes of that point.
Wre now come to the second point, with respect to the setting up of the committee of supply. I said to the right hon. gentleman the other evening that as no objection had been taken to setting up the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means the Minister of Finance moved that these two
committees toe set up. No objection was taken by any member of this house to that being done. The right hon. gentleman the other evening said that possibly the apposition had overlooked doing so. I told him that we had considered the matter before making the motion. I at once admitted that it is open to argument as to whether or not that committee could toe set up before we had passed the address. I shall come presently to the reasons why in this house I think it should be done. I said a moment ago that there is a distinction between the rules in the British house and those in our own in some minor particulars; the broad principle being, of course, that this house makes its own rules having regard to its own peculiar conditions. It will be within the memory of members of this house that Wednesday is a private members' day, it is a short day; Monday is a private members' day, a long day; Thursday is a private members' day for the first month. We have a rule, recently adopted, that when the house goes into supply on Thursday and Friday no motion is made; without motion the Speaker leaves the chair automatically on supply being called at the table. But there is one thing to be remembered; that cannot happen until such time as there has been opportunity for the house to discuss the broad question involved in the Speaker leaving the chair in order that consideration might be given to the items of any particular department. In other words when the Speaker automatically leaves the chair on supply being called on Thursday or Friday the house in committee cannot consider the items of any department that have not been previously considered, so that opportunity may be given for a motion of censure, if desired, against the minister and his administration of that department. Now as Thursday for the first month is a private members' day it follows that when private members' business is disposed of the Speaker leaves the chair on supply being called. But as it can only be with respect to departments that have not previously had items not passed, but considered, it follows that there must have been opportunity on motion made for the house to go into committee of supply to enable supply to be discussed.
The only day remaining for the first month is Tuesday. That is the reason for this motion, that is the distinction between the British rules and ours. In this house Tuesday is the only day remaining for the first month, if the business of the house is proceeded with as usual; that is, if private members take up all the sittings on Monday and on Wed-

Business of the House-Procedure
nesday, on Friday the Speaker can only leave the chair if there has been an antecedent discussion in committee of the items in supply that have to be dealt with by the committee. Unless on Tuesday the motion is made for the Speaker to leave the chair, while the house can go into supply on Friday, it cannot discuss any item because there has been no motion to have him leave the chair. There is no such rule as that in England. This is to meet this country's convenience, the purpose for which all rules are made. But I said to the right hon. gentleman and to this house, we do not ask this committee to pass a single item of supply, we only ask one thing, namely that there should be a formal going into committee of supply in order that an item may be called, as I said, in Finance, in Justice, or in Public Works; not passing them, but considering them, however trifling may be the item, in order that when Thursday and Friday come this house can go on with its business of supply with respect to the various items of the departments I have named that have to be dealt with. Is business to be expedited by the rules or retarded? Are the rules for the house or is the house for the rules? Were the rules made by the house or was the house by the rules? The rules were made by this chamber; and the rule making Tuesday the only day during the first month in which this matter can be dealt with is the reason for dealing with it as we have.
I will not repeat the argument that has been made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) as to the construction to be placed upon the rule. I said frankly the other night that that rule is open to the construction urged by the right hon. gentleman. I put upon it the construction that we did the other evening for the reason that, read with the other rule-and you must read all rules together to make sense out of them, that is the elementary rule of construction-as the first month of the sittings of this house is given up on Thursdays to private members, if the business of private members is exhausted on that day then we must have taken an antecedent step on Tuesday to deal with that situation.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the explanation of this whole matter. This government is in the hands of the house always with respect to the conduct of its business. Always. When we move adjournments, when we move that a certain step be taken to expedite the business, unanimity must be secured in order that business may be transacted. In this instance, read-

ing those two rules together, the setting up of the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means is a matter of which this house has supreme and complete control, and if there were any necessity for relying upon the fact that unanimous action was taken, the validity of the action cannot be challenged. It may well be that had the right hon. gentleman interposed and said, I object to that being done because this rule does not contemplate it, this argument could have been made then rather than now. But now clearly this house is estopped from asserting, and cannot now assert, that the rules have been contravened, for what it did it did with unanimity and the unanimous consent of this house is all that is required to abrogate any rule, to set up a new rule, to do any class of business we think best for the public good and to expedite the transaction of that business. In the closing days of the session, by unanimous consent we do practically everything.
The other question that is raised, whether or not we should pass supply before the governor's speech has been approved by this house, is of course another matter altogether. I am not one who does not realize the force of the argument that has been made against the passing of supply until such time as the speech has been adopted. But on the other hand we must read the rules together for the purpose of enabling business to be transacted. It would just mean that unless on Thursday and Friday we have the business of the house in such a position that the Speaker may leave the chair, and that means antecedent discussion here on the tabling of some items although they are not passed, then that use of the rules would be to prevent business being properly discharged. I submit to the house that that was was not the intention of the rule; that you must read that rule that permits the Speaker to leave the chair without motion put on these two days as a rule to expedite business. But if it comes on during the first month it retards it, unless we take the step we have taken. The only way in which it can be dealt with during the first month is to make a motion on a Tuesday, apparently. That is the position.
If this chamber thinks for a moment that there has been any effort on the part of the government to take rights from members, to deprive them of their privilege, I can assure them that such is not the case. It is so easy to make statements of that kind. I recall in this chamber that as a matter of convenience we have had the Speaker leave the chair on a Thursday or Friday, reserving the right to do so. The question of how we transact busi-

Business of the House-Procedure
ness is a matter of how we can best serve the purpose for which we are here, namely expeditiously getting through the business we have to do. Need I say that I vigorously deny the suggestion that anyone is endeavouring to push the business of the house more rapidly than it should be done. I think on reflection the right hon. gentleman will agree with me when I say that is an unwarranted observation.

speechtext:
No. If a question arises that indicates lack of unanimity then the Speaker must act, but frequently the rules of the house are set aside by unanimous consent. In the closing hours of every session we would not get through in a week the business we finish in a day or two if it were not that
we unanimously agree to the suspension of the rules. The Speaker of the house is the custodian of the rules of the house only to the extent to which the house shows, by lack of unanimity, that it desires him to apply the rules. If this house unanimously resolved this afternoon, on a motion made by any member, that we should adjourn until next Monday, on the adoption of that motion the Speaker would be 'bound to adjourn the house. He is the presiding officer; it is his duty to apply the rules which we ourselves have formed for the transaction of our business and our conduct in regard to that business.
I again assure the right hon. gentleman and every hon. member of this house that the endeavour to go into supply this afternoon [DOT] not to pass an item of supply-in my judgment is not a contravention of the rules, but rather is an application of the rules to the peculiar conditions that arise in this house by reason of the distribution of business, which make it essential that we go info and out of supply, not to pass items but to have it said that we have considered them, in order that the Speaker may leave the chair on Thursdays and Fridays in accordance with the provisions of the rule. There is no case to which my attention has been directed in which the house in Great [DOT] Britain has gone into supply before the adoption of the speech from the throne. I tell my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that there may be such cases, but I am not aware of them at the moment. In any case that would not have any effect upon the rules of this house, which have been established for the orderly conduct of its affairs in order to expedite the conduct of public business.

subtopic: COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY AND WAYS AND MEANS BEFORE ADDRESS AGREED TO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity of seeing these rules changed many times. In the old days one of the greatest grievances in this house was that on the orders of the day some members would arise and begin a discussion that would last during the entire sitting. We changed the rules to oblige the man who wanted to bring up something that was not on the order, paper; he could give notice thereof to the Speaker, and upon securing the consent of the house he could break away from the order paper to bring up the particular matter he wanted to discuss.
Further changes in regard to going into supply were made by Sir Robert Borden during the war, because then it was necessary to go into supply very often during the week to vote money. For that reason the rule was adopted that any item called on Tuesday

Business of the House-Procedure
could be gone on with on Thursday and Friday, when the Speaker would leave the chair without the question being put. I believe there is a great deal of support for that contention, which I think is generally approved of now by everyone in the house.
With regard to the right of the government to call the business in the order they wish, of course they have that power, always subject to the rules of the house. I have great respect for the rules of the British House of Commons, but the rules of this house prevail before those of the British house can be invoked. I remember a very knotty question that was brought up by the then young member for Portage la Prairie, now Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. He raised the point that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, having been elected for two seats, had to take the option within thirty days of sitting for one seat or the other, and he im'oked the first of our rules which states that in all unprovided cases the rules in England must apply. That question was hurled at me without notice, and I called upon Hon. Mr. Aylesworth, then Minister of Justice, to come to my assistance. After some research we found that this was a sessional rule in England, and the question to be determined was whether or not on July 1, 1867, the first day of the existence of the dominion, the British House of Commons was in session. It so happened that it was not in session on that date, and therefore the rule of the British house did not apply here. That, of course, enabled me to declare that the point of order raised by the then member for Portage la Prairie was not well taken. I remember that at the same time Sir Wilfrid Laurier remarked that evidently Mr. Meighen was a painstaking member with a future in the house.
As I have said, and as the house knows, the government has the right to call up business as it chooses, always according to the rules of the house. Time and again the rules are suspended; you can do that the moment you have unanimous consent, but in this connection I would direct the attention of the right hon. the Prime Minister to the fact that grievance before supply is the cardinal principle of our British constitution. The right of this government to carry on business has been challenged by a motion presented by the right hon. leader of the opposition as well as by a motion presented by the third party in this house. Before going into supply I believe the principle of grievance before supply should apply; the government should show the house and the country that it possesses the confidence of the house, and the only way to do this is to proceed with the

address and have these amendments voted down. The Prime Minister says that calling an item on Tuesday, even if it is not passed, does not mean that we are breaking away from the custom or doing away with the practice, but what does it mean? It means that if we call an item on Tuesday Your Honour will leave the chair automatically on Thursday and Friday, and then we might go on and vote millions, though the authority of the government has been challenged by two motions that are now before the house.
Taking all the circumstances into consideration, Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister, who is a great admirer of the British constitution and who gave us some very interesting information to-day, should have these motions disposed of before we take up supply at all.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on the point of order raised by my right hon. leader. Prime Minister were directed to standing order 28 rather than to standing order 57. I agree with the right hon. gentleman that a few nights a.go the question of the construction of standing order 28 came up in regard to the proper procedure in this house on Thursdays and Fridays, and I want to remind the right hon. gentleman, when he speaks of expediting the business of this house, that through its leader this party assured him the other day that if the debate on the address were disposed of the way it should be, according to the constitutional authorities, then we would meet his wishes and would not raise these technical objections in regard to going into supply on Thursdays and Fridays. So that the whole argument carefully built up by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in regard to expediting the public business of the country is disposed of, and the suggestions made from these benches have been disregarded. What is the point of order? The point of order centres around one standing order, and one only. I refer to standing order 57 of the House of Commons. The hon. member who has just preceded me properly mentioned that British rules do not apply in this House of Commons where our own specific rules do apply. Therefore I suggest with all respect that we have in regard to [DOT]rule 57 a Canadian interpretation. There is an interpretation by Bourinot, and so far as

Business oj the House-Procedure
I am concerned we do not have to go beyond the language of Bourinot to construe and interpret the significance of standing order 57. If Bourinot did not so express himself in the quotation read by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) then Redlich and other constituted authorities would prevail.
There are two questions at issue in this instance; one is in regard to the proper procedure in connection with the disposal of the address in reply, and the second question is -and by the way, it has not been answered -can this House of Commons go into committee of supply before we have disposed of the address in reply to the speech from the throne? speechtext:
The point of order has
been raised as to the meaning of standing order 57, it reads:
The house shall appoint the committees of supply, and ways and means, at the commencement of every session, so soon as an address has been agreed to in answer to His Excellency's speech.
Standing order 57 does not prevent the house appointing committees of supply and ways and means before the address in answer to His Excellency's address has been agreed to. As to whether such committees shall so be set up is a matter to be decided by the house, and not by the Speaker.
On February 20, 1930, it was resolved by this House of Commons:
That the speech of His Excellency the (governor General to both houses of parliament be taken into consideration on Monday next, and that this order have precedence over all business except the introduction of bills until disposed of.
At the fall session of 1930 no similar resolution was adopted. At the sessions of 1931, 1932 and 1933 consideration of the address was not given precedence. It was interrupted, and without objection other business was proceeded with by the house. On January 26, 1934, this session the house adopted the following resolution, on motion of Mr. Rhodes:
That this house will on Monday next resolve itself into a committee to consider of a supply to be granted to His Majesty.
There was a further resolution on motion by Mr. Rhodes as follows:
That this house will on Monday next resolve itselt into a committee to consider of the ways and means for raising the supply to be granted to His Majesty.
On motion of Mr. Rhodes the message of His Excellency the Governor General, together with the estimates presented were referred to committee of supply. In the present session the house has proceeded in the same manner as it has in the past three sessions. Whether that procedure shall continue is a matter entirely for the house to say.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the attitude of the right hon. gentleman is to be commended, but he has overlooked one thing and that is this, that there is no rule in Westminster similar to our rule about Thursday and Friday and as to Thursday being set aside for a special purpose during the first month. I say frankly, as I said to my colleague to my left, the real position is that the rules certainly conflict, and there is no way in which they can be brought into a proper logical scheme unless they are amended.
I perfectly appreciate the point which has been made and I understand it, but on the other hand, with this special rule in the

Silver Agreement
Canadian parliament about Thursday and Friday, and Thursday being a day set aside for the first month for a special purpose, it makes a situation that I cannot see how you can get over except in the way that I have indicated.
While I appreciate what the right hon. gentleman has said as to the dispatch of business, he realizes better than most members of the house, from his past experience, that any one member of the house not associated with him in the conduct of the opposition could raise an objection that would be fatal to that action on Friday. That is the real difficulty, and it was to overcome that difficulty that I made the suggestion that the Speaker should leave the chair.
So far as making a precedent is concerned, it is not making a precedent; it is conforming the practice of the house to the rules laid down about Thursday and Friday and as to Thursday being private members' day for the first month. There is a conflict which I see no way of keeping out of except in the manner I have suggested, and still do public business. I am perfectly willing that there should be a conference as to how the difficulty can be properly overcome, and in order that there might be no difficulty I suggested that the Speaker leave the chair. It is only a matter of five minutes to consider an item, and then we would go on with the next order of business. I only desire to have the business of the house done in the proper way.

speechtext: The hon. member had better put his question on the order paper.
Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend the Precious Metals Marking Act, 1928.
I understand that the minister already explained that this is merely a consolidation and revision of the existing act, and that he will explain the details in committee.
Yes.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions.

What are the
changes here?

There is a very slight change. The words "importer of" have been added, and the words "who traffics in" have been substituted for the word "dealer". It is in order to clarify. This was asked for unanimously by dealers in this class of goods.
Jewellers, are they?
Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Mount.

What is the
explanation of this section?

On certain silver or silver plated ware and gold and gold plated ware, there are sometimes what are called mounts, that is, a design or some other decoration which is superimposed. These mounts have never been properly defined under the act and this new section clarifies this matter and provides for the application of the terms of the act to the things mounted upon the plate itself. In other words, it is making the regulations apply to the parts mounted upon the plate the same as they apply to the plate itself.

Section agreed to.

On section 3-Gold. National mark.
Will the minister explain this section?

The section reads "composed
of gold of not less than nine carats in fineness,"' and I should like to know if this regulation is in effect in other countries.
I think that is the standard minimum recognized in the trade.

The explanatory note reads:
This proposed national mark on gold and silver articles (not gold plated or silver plated) should stimulate both the buying and manufacturing of gold and silver articles in Canada.
Will the minister explain how this effect-will be brought about by this proposal?

It is expected that the
addition of this section will stimulate the art of producing gold and silverware. A very fine business in an artistic way has been developed in this country, particularly in silverware. In years gone by certain countries in Europe-Great Britain has been an outstanding case-developed a definite skill in this art and turned out some very fine ware. Canada, being a new country, has not been particularly forward up until say the last fifteen or twenty years. But in that period the artistic production of gold and silver in Canada has been very material. We are now second in the production of gold and I think third in the production of silver and this country lends itself to the production of gold and silverware. The trade generally has been unanimous in asking for this amendment in order to set a standard in this country for these wares.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Silver. National mark.
The same argument applies to this section as was applied to the preceding section.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-Gold plated and silver plated articles.
What is the reason for this?

This section is intended
to make more clear the regulations covering Sheffield reproductions. In other words, there are certain wares known the world over as Sheffield and the term "Sheffield reproduction" has been used in this and other countries. The natural inference is that the article produced

Precious Metals Marking Act
is of similar quality and standard to that generally produced in Sheffield. In the absence of more specific regulations, certain manufacturers have impinged somewhat upon the standard by producing an inferior article. It is to clarify the situation that these amendments have been made. In other words, when the public buy a Canadian article termed a Sheffield reproduction, it will know it is getting an article just as good as the original article.
What is the penalty under the act?
We do not touch the penalties in this amendment. They are not what I would call stiff but are suited to the case. Frequent prosecutions are undertaken by the officer administering the act.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Gold.
What is the regulation dated December 6, 1928?

It will be observed that subsection (7) of this section is very technical but this amendment is simply to transpose into the act a regulation which has been in force for some years. What is sought to be done by this section has previously been done under the general powers to pass regulations not inconsistent with the act. The officers administering the act have at times found themselves embarrassed with the challenge that the regulation might exceed their powers in some technical detail. Therefore, it was thought advisable that the full definition should be carried into the act, and this is done by subsection (7). This subsection is highly technical but it has been gone over with great care by the officers of this and the justice department, all of which are agreed as to the correctness of the definition and its necessity and soundness.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-Obligatory marks.
What is the effect of this section?

Part of the Trade Mark and Design Act was repealed and in its place was passed what is known as the Unfair Competition Act, 1932. This section formerly appeared in that part of the Trade Mark and Design Act which was repealed and now is being brought under the authority of the Unfair Competition Act, 1932. It is merely a technical amendment.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-Electro-plated flat-ware.
What will be the probable effect of this section upon prices?

I would say that there will be no effect upon prices. This section merely clarifies a matter which has been in dispute for some time. Hon. members know that in recent years there has grown up a large sale in cheap and imitation jewelery and stuff of that character. Young girls like this for decorative purposes and we have been told that some of it is a very fine reproduction of real gold, silver, platinum and other precious metals. All we are concerned about is to make certain that no such product is imported and sold or made here and sold as platinum, gold, silver or plated-ware. The new sections 11 and 11A are designed to clarify the law in regard to these practices. It will not add to the price. In other words, it will not affect cheap jewelery at all, so long as such jewelery does not presume to be what it is not, namely, 14 karat gold or whatever it may be, nor profess to be sterling silver or silver-plated when in fact it is not. In gold plate there is a certain base of weight in gold that must be actually in the ware before it can bear the stamp "Gold Plated," and in silverware there must be a copper or nickel base and a specified quantity of silver in the article in proportion to that base before the article can carry the term "Silver Plated." Anything that does not meet with these regulations cannot bear the stamp "Silver Plated" or "Gold Plated," as the case may be.

Section agreed to.
On section 9-Meaning.

This deals with the nomenclature of the trade and the symbols used- "R.P." for rolled plate, and so forth, as set forth. It is merely to legalize these letters, because on small articles like a ring, for instance, there is not room to stamp the words "Rolled Plate", and the letters will be sufficient. This section specifies the terms that may be used and the meanings attaching to the letters in each case.

In every newspaper one
picks up there are advertisements for the buying of gold jewelery of various kinds. Is there any law in this regard?

A very strict law. The
whole act, including what we have been considering to-day, applies to such matters. Not frequently but occasionally our officers come
Intoxicating Liquors Act

across false advertising. Such advertisements are carefully scrutinized and where there are grounds for prosecution the offenders are prosecuted. The practice of misrepresentation in regard to cheap jewelery is very sharply dealt with by the officers.

Is there any provision for
protecting the public with respect to prices paid for jewelery they sell, or are the prices left to the buyer himself?

Competition between the
manufacturer and the importer of what might be called legitimate jewelery is naturally very sharp. In the five and ten cent stores and in the department stores there is extensive and keen competition in the sale of the class of jewelery to which the hon. gentleman refers, and so long as such jewelery does not carry deceptive markings we do not interfere. Our duty under the act is to see that the public are not deceived.

Section agreed to.
Section 10 agreed to.
On section 11-Offence.

What is the
penalty? The offence might be minor and the penalty severe.

This subsection is an addition to a number of others all coming within the same category of penalties. I cannot inform my hon. friend at the moment what the penalties are, but they are not severe, nor have I ever heard anyone complain about them. I suppose that anyone who is penalized naturally thinks the penalty severe, but I have never heard any complaints in this regard.
Mr. MACKENZiE (Vancouver): They are all fines?
Yes.
I suppose these amendments were asked for and approved by the Canadian Jewelers' Association. What percentage of the jewelers belong to the association?
Practically all-all reputable concerns. I do not know of any exceptions, and certainly none have been taken.
