City of Ottawa Agreement

Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That, it is expedient to authorize the Minister of Public Works, on behalf of His Majesty, to tenter into an agreement with the corporation of the city of Ottawa to extend the period of the existing agreement with the corporation for one year from July 1, 1933.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
May I ask the minister if it is his intention to introduce a bill based on this resolution, if carried?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, it is necessary to do so in order to make payments out of the consolidated revenue fund.
Will the minister explain the nature of the measure?

The proposition
is simply to continue an arrangement that has been in existence for some years past between the government and the city of Ottawa with respect to certain services, and the supply of water at the same rates as have been paid for some years. This agreement was made some ten years ago, I think, and amended while my right hon. friend was Prime Minister, and for the last three or four years it has simply been continued at the same rate, $100,000 per year for water. There is nothing else involved. Many of the questions that arose under the agreement have been settled from time to time and have passed out of the realm of practical matters, and this really applies only to the payment of $100,000 per year for water.

I do not know, Mr. Chairman, whether this is the moment to discuss the broader question of the relations of the city and the government, but I would like to suggest to the minister that when he is taking up with the city council of Ottawa the question of an agreement between the government and the city he seek to impress upon His Worship the Mayor and the members of the council that something besides the mere letter of agreements is worthy of consideration between large bodies such as the government of Canada and the corporation of the city of Ottawa. As the minister well knows, the government of Canada at very considerable expense expropriated certain pro-74726-20
perties in the city of Ottawa for the purposes of a national park. Before doing so there were conferences between the city and the government as to the extent to which cooperation between the two might obtain in accordance with a generally understood plan. In a word the plan was that a large area in the centre of the city should be set aside as a park to be designated Confederation park, as a permanent memorial to the celebration of the diamond jubilee of confederation. Before any move was made by the federal government, as my hon. friend well knows it was necessary to call into conference the mayor and certain members of the board of control of the city at the time, and secure their general agreement to the plan. It involved action on the part of the city as well as on the part of the government. As far as the government was concerned the carrying out of the plan involved the expropriation of large areas of property in the heart of the city, and paying, I think, over $3,000,000 for properties to be demolished in order that the city which is also the capital might be provided in part with the proposed park. The city itself also undertook to make certain expropriations, and among other things did carry out an agreement to widen a considerable portion of Elgin street so as to permit of the park having a very wide street on the west as an approach to the parliament buildings.
In the course of consideration of the whole plan the question came up as to what was to be done with the few buildings remaining within the area it was proposed to set aside for the park; that area being bounded by Elgin street on the west, the canal on the east-or rather the street just beyond the canal on the east side, I have forgotten the name for the moment-
Nicholas street.

Yes, Nicholas street, and Sparks or Wellington street on the north and Lisgar street, I think, on the south, I mean the far side of Cartier square where the Normal school is at present located. As hon. members will recognize, already most of that is in the nature of park area, and the question came up as to what would be done with buildings that might still remain within it as the time drew near for their being demolished. While there was not a written underbaking with respect to what would be done in that regard, the understanding was that no new buildings should be allowed to be erected within that area, and that as far as the city hall itself was concerned, if the time came that it was to be

City o) Ottawa Agreement

taken down or demolished, that location would fall into the general park area. As I was Prime Minister at the time and had to do directly with the negotiations, in which the federal district commission was also concerned, I would like to make it quite clear that there was no doubt in the minds of His Worship the Mayor and the board of control and the city council at the time or of the federal district commission or of the government of the day as to what the understanding was and the basis on which the government proceeded to make the expropriations which it did. Certainly if there had been any possibility of the city not cooperating in a wholehearted manner with the government in the improvement of the capital along the lines laid down, the government of that day would not have asked parliament to appropriate 83,000,000 or thereabouts for the expropriation of an area which lies right within the heart of the city.
The point I wish to make is this: the mayor and city council of Ottawa at the present time have called for designs for a new city hall.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: On the old site?

Well the intimation is that the design should relate to the old site, but I understand that His Worship the Mayor has made it clear that that is more for the purpose of getting designs which will enable the city council to form estimates of what such a building would cost than actually to fix the location of the new building. I think the idea is to get the estimates at once for a building of a certain size, but not finally to decide upon a site until there have been further conferences with the government. That is my reason for mentioning at the moment what my understanding is of the arrangement made between the city and the government at the time the government asked this parliament to appropriate large sums of money for the expropriating of certain properties.
I should like to ask the government to stress with the city, if they will, the point that the object of the park is to provide a great open centre which will be not only an adornment to the capital of Canada but also something of practical service to the citizens of Ottawa, who are equally concerned in having a central park which can be used for ceremonial and other occasions and for gatherings of different kinds not to speak of the day to day use by children, young people, and persons of all ages. There is a civic end as well as a government end to be served,

and I should like to point out that there would be as much justification for the government taking the properties that it owns to-day in the park area and beginning to erect government buildings on them as there is for the city to claim the city hall site' as the one on which to construct a new city hall, since that site comes within the park area.
The government has expropriated all the land along the west side of the canal between Sparks street and Laurier avenue; it has constructed a fine driveway there of which the city has the advantage to-day. That drive is being maintained by the federal district commission. If the government of Canada were to take the ground that merely because they owned that land they could put up buildings within the park area, they would be perfectly justified in building on that roadway. They would be equally justified in putting up large public buildings in the area between Wellington and Sparks street, between the post office and Elgin street and south of Sparks street between the city hall site and Sparks street. The government of Canada would have as much justification for using land which it owns and which it has thrown into a genaral park scheme as the civic authorities have in claiming for building purposes the use of the south side of the old city hall which now has come into the park area. As a matter of fact as yet the civic authorities have not carried out a part of their specific agreement which was set out in writing, calling for the removal of the fire hall and police station from the park area. That should have been done years ago in accordance with the terms of the agreement.
This whole matter has relation to a plan in which all the governments of Canada have been interested and will continue to be interested. The government of Sir Robert Borden appointed a commission which went very carefully into the whole question of the future planning of the capital, and that commission recommended a large park in the centre of the city. The Liberal government which succeeded the Conservative administration of that day sought to carry on the plans of improvement of the capital that had been initiated and commenced by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and continued by the government of Sir Robert Borden. I hope the minister will impress upon the city authorities the fact that in these negotiations between the city and the government there are larger considerations involved than just the matter of one small site.
I should like to add this, that I am sure this parliament will wish to be generous within reason with the city of Ottawa. That has

City oj Ottawa Agreement
been the attitude of parliament in the past and I am sure it will be so in the future, but parliament will expect a like attitude on the part of the city authorities. I hope it may be possible for the government, through its negotiations, to complete some arrangement which will ensure that the park area will be preserved as originally intended, and which will also enable the city to carry out some plan with regard to the erection of a city hall in connection with a scheme which will have the full approval of the administration of the day.

Mr. Chairman, as one
whose honour and privilege it is to represent the capital city of this dominion, in association with my colleague, may I be permitted to associate myself with the remarks just made by my right hon. leader. Though the city of Ottawa belongs to its citizens it also belongs to the whole of Canada as its capital city. On a former occasion, when it was my privilege to speak with regard to the construction of the Victory Tower, I think Hansard will bear out that I said that the construction should be such as to represent the desires, the ambitions and the hopes of the Canadian nation so that the tower might in some way represent all these sentiments.
I do not know what the intention of the government may be with regard to the city of Ottawa, but I would ask that the government should not forget that Ottawa is the capital city of Canada, and that to it come legislators from the various provinces of Canada and visitors from the four corners of the earth. So I think that the government should do everything within reason, even in these very distressing times, to make the capital city of the dominion well worthy of the ambition, the courage and the fortitude of the Canadian nation, of which the right hon. Prime Minister is so wont to speak. When that time comes when the government feel like spending something, I would ask them to consider the fact 'that as one of the representatives of the city of Ottawa I have urged that this is one city that ought to be recognized throughout Canada.

In reply to my
right hon. friend I can only say that I have reviewed the file of correspondence and representations in connection with the park area to which he has referred, and undoubtedly he has interpreted that correspondence quite properly. There have not been any recent negotiations with the city in connection with the proposed construction of a city hall on the old site, so all I know is what I have 74726-20J
read in the press. From those reports I would expect that in the future there might be some discussion of this matter, and certainly I shall bring to the attention of the representatives of the city on such occasions the contentions and representations that have been made by my right hon. friend, because he has been thoroughly familiar with the matter since its inception.
Bound up with this matter is more than simply the opening of a park area. We must consider also the location of the national monument and other questions which undoubtedly, in the near future, will call for a conference between the government and the city. I can only say that we have endeavoured to arrive at a conclusion that is in the best interests of the Dominion of Canada and of the city, and that is calculated to carry out the original intention, so far as possible, as it is expressed in the correspondence.
I can only add that by this legislation we cannot in any way deal with the matters mentioned by my right 'hon. friend; the act has no application whatever to anything of that kind, since it deals only with certain services for which we make an annual payment.

speechtext: I think it only proper to say that some time ago we set up a committee of council consisting of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart), the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) and Sir George Perley to consider this whole matter. Certainly there is no agreement and there would seem to be nothing in the nature of an arrangement which bound the city with respect to the rebuilding of the city hall so far as we can ascertain. I speak subject to correction with respect to that. There seemed to be however an understanding that the park was to be continued through to Cartier square. I believe expropriation proceedings were taken by the city with respect to the area which lies to the west of the Roxborough apartment.
That is right.

Also, the property which lies to the north of that was expropriated leaving, as the right hon. gentleman has said, the fire hall, which is still on city property so far as I have been able to ascertain.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, February 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gobeil for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, the amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Gardiner.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before an hon. member proceeds to speak in the debate I should like to make some observations. Mr. Gobeil moved:
That an address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General to offer the humble thanks of this house to His Excellency for the gracious speech which he has been pleased to make to both houses of parliament.
Mr. Mackenzie King moved in amendment:
That the following be added to the motion: We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers do not possess the confidence of the country.
Mr. Gardiner moved:
That the amendment be amended by inserting after the word " advisers " the words " and official opposition."
Mr. Gardiner in moving the amendment to the amendment is reported at page 105 of Hansard of January 30, as follows:
The amendment as amended would then read: "We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers and official opposition do not possess the confidence of this house or of the country.
The hon. member was mistaken in stating that the amendment to the amendment would so read. He has not moved to add the words "of this house or," and they are not contained in Mr. Mackenzie King's
(.Mr. Bennett.]
amendment. If the subamendment were adopted it would make the amendment read as follows:
That the following be added to the motion: " We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers and official opposition do not possess the confidence of the country.
The adoption of the subamendment would make the amendment a motion of want of confidence in the official opposition. Members of the official opposition are but individual members, and are not charged with the duty of advising His Excellency. The question as to whether or not the official opposition has or has not the confidence of the public is settled by the mere fact that it is the opposition. It is immaterial that His Excellency be made aware at the present time whether the official opposition or any other party or group has or has not the confidence of the public as long as the government of the day has the support of a majority of the House of Commons. Of this fact His Excellency has been officially advised.
If a vote of want of confidence in a government is carried it means the resignation of the government, His Excellency's advisers. On the other hand a vote of want of confidence in the opposition is of no effect and not a matter to be submitted to His Excellency. It is a well known principle of British parliamentary practice that votes of want of confidence are directed only against the government of the day. I therefore declare the subamendment out of order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that it has been decided to go ahead with the debate on the address I am permitted to get my little say off my chest two or three days sooner than I had anticipated. For that I am very grateful.
Turning to the speech from the throne I have much pleasure in announcing that I believe I shall be able to support one of the important measures forecast, namely legislation to facilitate the efficient and profitable marketing of live stock and agricultural products. I shall support it particularly if it lives up to the forecast contained in the press as to what is to be the nature of such legislation. I understand it is to be patterned after the British Agricultural Marketing Act of 1931 which I have in my hand. If Canadian legislation follows the British it will greatly facilitate the marketing of live stock and other farm products.
I regret however that, apparently deliberately, the government allowed a first class marketing medium to die right before its

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
eyes. I refer to the Cooperative Live Stock Association established in 1928, the operations of which extended across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, which had done a very important commission business for a number of years and had just nicely got into the export trade. This Canadian organization had first class connection with the Scottish Cooperative Association in Edinburgh, but it was struck amidships first by adverse exchange in September, 1931, and then by the fact that the government reduced the grant by S10,000. These two unfortunate circumstances combined to put this institution on the rocks.
It was therefore up to the government to do something in connection with the marketing of live stock, and apparently it is about to do something, although it is a little late. I do not know whether or not the Cooperative Live Stock Association, to which I have referred, is still alive, but certainly it is not functioning as an export institution.
I shall not deal at length with the wheat agreement; I should like to see it first. May I tell the government that there is considerable opposition growing up throughout the country against such an agreement. I should not like to take the stand some people are taking. Although I have read Premier Bracken's first class presentation of the subject, I do not quite see how it can work out. Possibly however as time goes on we will get more light on the subject. I am going to enumerate a number of blunders, from our standpoint, which the government has made during the last four or five years in the disposition and marketing of our grain, and in their attempts to stabilize this, that and the other thing. Nearly every attempt made by any country to do something spectacular of an artificial nature, which I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) does not agree with very much on general principles, to try to get us out of the difficult position we are in has been a failure, and this government's record in this respect is not dissimilar to that of any other country-possibly a little bit worse.
The first matter to which I wish to refer is the Prime Minister's entry into the interimperial field of diplomacy in 1930. We all remember that he went to London on October 1, after having first shoved up the duties on many British goods. Then he promenaded to London and announced that he had arrived. Let me refer for a moment to the Prime Minister's first speech, I think it was, in England, and remember, he was proceeding to carry out his blasting and blazing
policy at that time. After first slapping the British people, his kinsmen, in the face by shoving up the tariff on a number of British commodities he announced this:
We must approve or reject the principle. I have put the question definitely to you and definitely it should be answered.
He not only intimates there how he is going to apeak but suggests how they should reply. He went on:
There is here no room for compromise, and there is no possibility of avoiding the issue.
You would think our kinsmen over there were trying to dodge him. He continued:
Ihis is a time for plain speaking, and I speak plainly when I say that the day is now at hand when the peoples of the empire must decide, once and for all, whether our welfare lies in closer economic union or whether it does not. Delay is hazardous, further discussion of the principle is surely unnecessary. The time for action has come.
_ Well, if that is the new diplomacy, if that is the policy of blasting and blazing, and I think apparently it was, results came immediately which resulted in our premier coming home empty handed. Before he was in London eight days, I think it was exactly on the eighth day, the Prime Minister let all and sundry know that " where MacGregor sat, that was the head of the table." He was on the radio talking to the world, instead of engaging in a conference. That is such a painful incident that I will leave it with that historic remark of Hon. Mr. Thomas- "humbug." I shall not try to paint the lily. That was major blunder No. 1 in 1930.
In 1931 there was another big blunder, although affecting a relatively small number of people in Saskatchewan. That was when the government undertook to give a five cent bonus on wheat to the growers of the west. It was spoken of first as a compensating adjustment, but it was in the nature of relief or bonus and it followed a very excellent speech made by the Prime Minister on July 1, 1931, in which he announced to the people of Canada the calamity that had struck the western plains because of the drought in that area. But imagine the consternation of the people when they found that to those who had had a fine crop this government disbursed over 811,000,000, and the bigger the crop the more of a bonus the farmer got; while on the other hand, those who had no crop at all or very little got nothing which they did not have to pay back or give a promissory note for. That was the most amazing spectacle of stupidity and asininity in the whole administration of relief, and

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
nobody has ever even attempted to justify such a record. The municipalities in the southwest feeling strongly that they were entitled to some consideration when others were getting a cash handout, not something to be given back but a gift, a Christmas box, sent a deputation to Ottawa proposing that a bonus of one dollar per acre be given in the southern part of Saskatchewan, which was so hard hit on that occasion, and this was refused. That refusal was blunder No. 2-a most egregious and stupid blunder that no parliament of seventeen-year-old schoolboys would ever think of committing. I want to tell my hon. friends over there that that was one of the first things that caused the present government to take a terrible slide in the estimation and confidence of the people of the west. Everybody knew it was wrong. Even those who got the five cent bonus knew it was most unmercifully unjust to the southwesit and that is one of the many reasons why the government is rapidly sinking further and further in the estimation of the people of the west.
Then we had the Ottawa conference in 1932. Of course, there was no conference in 1931, or there would have been a more major blunder then. But there were conferences in the other three years. In 1932 a conference was called by the Prime Minister after consulting with the overseas dominions. Of course, we thought then, with the Prime Minister playing the part of host, that everything would be as nice as pie, that everything would be lovely. I think this was the very building the conference was held in. If one-half the reports we got were true, it was anything but a harmonious family gathering. But we will not dwell upon that. We all regret the rumours. Our Prime Minister did not come out of that conference with very great laurels upon his brow.
I want to refer to one statement that is being made ail over by the government and its supporters, and that is that we got a preference on our wheat which was tantamount to getting six cents a bushel more than we otherwise would have got. Out in the west the western Tory members are continually trying to leave that impression, although the Prime Minister said distinctly on October 12, 1932, that he had no thought of exacting six cents per bushel more from the homeland for our wheat, thereby adding to the cost of bread in the old country. Here are the Prime Minister's words, at page 135 of Hansard of October 12, 1932:
I have never at any time represented to the wheat growers of this country that the effect
[Mr. Motherwell.1
of a preference would be to set up in their favour a price differential in world markets and at the expense of the British consumer.
That is plain enough, yet the followers of the right hon. gentleman are continually stating out in the west that we get a preference which amounts to six cents a bushel for our wheat.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
misunderstood that. The Canadian producer does get six cents more than the foreigner gets for his wheat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It hits the foreigner but it does not help us. With the low value of foreign currencies, the foreigner has still the edge on us just the same. For fear that we might get a little bit out of that preference, look at the proviso in article 4 of the United Kingdom-Canada agreement. We get the preference provided we sell our wheat "at prices not exceeding the world prices." That is the proviso. Here are the terms of the contract. Of course, we know who put that in there and who agreed to it. It was Mr. Baldwin who put that in to protect himself when he went home, and the Prime Minister of this country wanted article 4 of the agreement so that he would be able to say that he got a preference for our wheat in the British market. But we get no better price. It is just the same as we have been getting for the last fifty years, and we can go on getting it for the next five years under this contract. Blunder number three.
What else took place in 1932? I think it was in 1932 that the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance), the hon. member for AVillow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) and the hon. member for AVeyburn (Mr. Young) raised the question as to the relationship between the government and Mr. John I. McFarland who was then operating on the Winnipeg grain exchange. I understand that primarily he went to that exchange as the representative of the pool, and whether or not they suggested it, I understand that that appointment was pleasing to the government. Things drifted on until Mr. McFarland became the hedging medium of almost the entire grain trade of Canada. That is the statement made by the Prime Minister in 1932, but prior to that his colleague had made the bold statement that Mr. McFarland was not dealing in wheat, either directly or indirectly, and was not on the market at all for the government. He said that Mr. McFarland was independent of parliament and of the government. What extraordinary statements to make! Who is this Goliath that is on the market and is independent of everyone, including the Prime

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
Minister? I wonder from whom he takes his orders? Does he take his orders from the pool or from the Prime Minister?
We find that since the fall of 1930 when Mr. McFarland began to stabilize the market, whatever that means, the stabilization has consisted in prices going down to the lowest point in four hundred years. Yet this gentleman was supposed to have authority not only to stabilize the Canadian market but to stabilize the world market. Those are his very words.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Whose words?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It did not stabilize-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Whose words are those?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). That stabilization process did not but momentarily keep up prices, but it did result in Canada hoarding her wheat until the carry-over was larger than ever before. I have some figures which I obtained from the pool at Regina and from what I know about them I consider them substantially correct. I want to establish that while the operations of Mr. John I. McFarland were well intended by the government, they resulted in prices going down to an all-time record. That is the admission made in a leaflet which has recently been got out by the federal and prairie governments. The yield during the last four years has been smaller but the carry-over in each year has been larger than in the preceding four years. The average total production for the crop years 1926, 1927, 1928 and 1929 was 439,000,000 bushels, while the average total production for the last four years, 1930, 1931, 1932 and 1933, under this government and under the stabilization of Mr. John I. McFarland, was only 368,000,000 bushels. The average production for the last four years was therefore 71,000,000 bushels less than the average production for the preceding four years. The carry-over for 1926 was 40,000,000 bushels; for 1927, 53,000,000 bushels; for 1928,
92,000,000 bushels and for 1929, 127,000,000 bushels, a total of 312,000,000 bushels. The carry-over for 1930 was 127,000,000 bushels; for 1931, 140,000,000 bushels; for 1932, 137,000,000 bushels and estimated for 1933, 219,000,000 bushels, a total of 623,000,000 bushels, so that the average carry-over for this four-year period, 1930 to 1933, was 155,000,000 bushels, or twice the amount of the average carry-over of the previous four-year period. These figures show that while the average annual production for the years 1930 to 1933 was 71,000,000 bushels less than it was for the years 1926 to 1929, the average annual carryover for 1930-33 was over 76,000,000 bushels in excess of the average annual carry-over for 1926-29.
I will admit that Mr. McFarland might be able to hold up the price of grain momentarily or temporarily; I will admit that he might do it for an hour or two a day or perhaps for twenty-four hours, but there are two things that will always happen when you try to hold up prices above those obtaining on the world's markets. One of two things, and perhaps both, will happen. Wheat will be thrown on the Winnipeg market from Chicago, or elsewhere the price will be beaten down and Mr. McFarland will be put in the position of endeavouring to do the impossible by holding up the market while great volumes of grain futures are thrown at him from all sides. The only result is what did happen,-down goes the price until it reaches a record low for the last four hundred years. That is one thing that will happen. The other is that the slight degree to which he holds up the market immediately loses us export opportunities. Everyone knows that the moment we get out of line with competing countries, exporting ceases or dwindles away to a mere dribble. This policy, begotten of the very best intentions, has resulted in doubling our carry-over in the face of smaller crops during the last four years. I hope I have made myself plain on this point because I do not want to dwell any longer upon it than is actually necessary.
In 1932 the government entered upon a program of fake preferences. They made good and sure that -we should not receive any benefit from them by putting in the contract the stipulation that we must sell as we have always been selling, at world prices. That policy and the apparently free-lance appointment of Mr. McFarland had regrettable reactions, but I do not feel like blaming the government too much for them. These policies did not bring the results anticipated for the simple reason that the Argentine and Australia were able to undersell Canada, even though their products were of an inferior grade. This was made possible because of their depreciated currencies. Now that Mr. McFarland is hedging almost the entire wheat crop it cannot be said any longer that he is acting personally for a company or for the pool. He has the credit of Canada behind him and I think this house is entitled to know exactly what he is doing. I have placed some questions upon the order paper but sufficient time has not elapsed to make a complaint about not receiving answers. My information is that Mr. McFarland is in the employ and the pay of the government. Anyway, he has an office and staff.

But with Mr. McFarland hoarding wheat, just as they hoarded wheat in the United States, it is no wonder North America gained the reputation of being hoarders of wheat, compelling buyers in Europe to turn 
to other sources for their supplies. It has been a huge blunder on the part of hon. gentlemen, who evidently do not know anything about their business in this respect. That is the trouble.

This is the time, we are told, to make complaints, to ventilate our grievances, and my constituents are anxious to have from the government an audited statement of the business of John I. McFarland during all these years. I will not take the responsibility of running into an election and admitting that I have not done anything to see that this matter has been thoroughly explained to the people, that they have not been made aware of the relationship of the government with Mr. McFarland and also with the pool. My information is that the original wheat which the pool turned over to Mr. McFarland has not yet been sold and accounted for to the pool. If that is so, and I believe it is, what a wonderful medium of getting rid of our wheat we have had all these years' They were going to show the pool how to sell wheat. Now, Mr. McFarland has occupied the position almost of a receiver. Well, he received the wheat, but he has not sold it-just transferred it into futures. He has not liquidated the pool wheat; and I understand that* not having done any of these things, he has really defaulted or been neglectful in his duties as receiver, so that it is up to the government, for their own sake as well as for Mr. McFarland's, to elucidate a little their relationship with Mr. McFarland and to let us know how much longer that gentleman proposes to keep up this hoarding policy. Is it going to be kept up until all the buyers in England are driven elsewhere for their supplies?
Hon. gentlemen may smile, but these are the seeming facts; and these carryover figures are correct. If they have anything further and fuller to offer us I am sure the house will be glad to know what it is. In the meantime I want it understood that we cannot allow this to run any longer. I cannot take the responsibility of not asking the government for some light on this subject-I will not say demanding; I will ask them for it. The Prime Minister two years ago made a very full statement, a good statement on the government's wheat stabilization policy. I do not know whether he understood it himself, but many of us did not.

That is the situation as I understand it. There may have been developments in the last two or three days, but with Russia out of the picture it is absolute folly to talk about restricting our wheat acreage and permitting them.to occupy our place. There is another factor to be taken into consideration in this connection, and that is that in addition to wheat all these countries grow rye. So that all that their farmer would have to do, even if compelled to reduce his acreage of wheat fifteen per cent, would be to grow that much more rye. Rye is made into bread-occasionally it is made into liquids but for the most part it is made into bread, and good bread, which is used almost entirely in some countries in Europe. The result is that you will have as many loaves of bread as ever, if no provision is being made here with respect to the non-growing of rye. That is another evidence that hon. gentlemen do not know their business with respect to the world grain situation. Suppose that is exaggerated; suppose half the people of the world go to bed hungry, what justification have we for reducing the present abundance in order to benefit those countries who have too much, and letting the other half of the world starve to death? You are just making C.C.F.'ers every day by following such a policy. And be it further resolved,-that the government of Canada take such steps as are necessary and expedient to explore the possibility and practicability of selling on long term credits a substantial quantity of our embarrassing wheat carry-over to China, or any other available country where poverty, hunger and misery prevail.
Three things may stand in the way of that being carried out. We had representatives from China trying to negotiate an arrangement with the government a year ago.

The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
I do not care where the wheat goes, whether to China or Japan or Russia, so long as it goes into consumption and we are not guilty either of destroying it or taking steps to prevent future abundance of it. So long as it goes to help someone and establishes a trade contact with some country that has not yet learned to use our wheat, it satisfies me. We want to develop a taste for wheat flour and wheat bread and get contacts with these countries with huge populations. We have to do it, whether we do it from a humanitarian or a business standpoint. We are being crowded out of Europe, and everyone knows the reason-their desire to become selfsustaining in the event of war, and in some measure justified retaliation against Canada for our high tariffs against them. So I suggest with all the earnestness the Prime Minister gave me credit for last year that disposition be made of our surplus wheat on the best terms possible to those hungry countries. It would of course add: a certain amount to the national debt of Canada. Suppose we add 875,000,000-and mark you, Mr. Speaker, we are responsible more than any other country in the world for this huge cany-over-in my estimation even if the government should add 850,000,000 or 875,000,000 to the public debt by taking this action I think it would have a better effect than will result from a reduction in acreage, and it would also bring about a new contact with a new country, establish a line of business which we do not have now and help cultivate a further taste for wheat bread. I can remember when Japan consumed very little wheat, while now she is a very large consumer, and it is the same with other countries. That is my alternative suggestion, and in addition I would say that the proposal advanced by the government is not workable. It is more apt to increase than decrease production, as experience has shown in the United States during the past twelve years.
I know that to many of our eastern friends the question of wheat is a complex problem, but I am going to point out that the government do not even know much about hogs. I have here the official hand-book of present conditions and recent progress in Canada for 1933. We have the picture of the Prime Minister in the front of the booklet, as large as life and twice as natural, and here we are told the kind of hogs we should grow, according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who goes on to elaborate on the great market that has been opened to us. Then directly below is shown a group or litter of twelve Yorkshire geldings, so called. What a fearful thing it is to fall into the hands of a government that knows nothing about either wheat or hogs. This pamphlet has gone to libraries in every part of the British Empire, Mr. Speaker. I know when I was in the department these bulletins went to every part of the world. Mr. Speaker, after extending my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the address, which I do most heartily, may I make the observation that several times since this government came into office have I said that it has done more for the farmers of this Dominion of Canada during the three or four years it has been in office than the Liberal government did in the whole nine years previously. The proof of that contention is found in the fact that to-day this government is receiving support for its policies from those gentlemen in the house who do not belong to either of the old parties. We see them rising one after the other and commending the government for what it has done and

is doing with respect to agriculture in this country.
My remarks this evening may be somewhat more fragmentary than usual because I desire to place on record some figures in opposition to some of the fancies that have been given utterance on the other side of the house to-day and in the past day or two. Before doing so however I wish to apply myself to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) the other day with regard to the relationship of the two central provinces to the western provinces of Canada in the matter of taxation. The hon. gentleman said that 45 per cent of the taxes of Canada were paid by the province of Ontario and 30 per cent by the province of Quebec. Had he said that 45 per cent of the taxes were paid in the province of Ontario he might have been within the mark; but when he says that they are paid by the province, that is an entirely different story. The great companies doing business throughout Canada have their headquarters in Montreal and Toronto to a large extent. The banks, for example, pay one per cent tax on circulation. That circulation is dominion-wide but the tax is paid in eastern Canada, and Ontario and Quebec try to take the credit for it. The great loan companies, the insurance companies, the railway companies and businesses with headquarters in eastern Canada all pay taxes in the east, but they make throughout the dominion the money out of which they pay those taxes. To say therefore that 75 per cent of the taxes in the country are paid by the two central provinces, and to leave that statement unmodified, does not present a true picture of the respective responsibilities of the different provinces of the dominion. The hon. member referred to the wheat pool and the agreements and guarantees. The guarantees will not cost the prairie provinces anything, because they are secured by mortgages on property, and the payments which the pool has agreed to make with respect to the guarantees will be made and continue to be made year by year.
With regard to railway policies, the western provinces have been no more guilty than any other part of the dominion. As regards social legislation, we have perhaps gone further than we ought to have done; but I should like anyone to name me any province that has not done the same. So far as balanced budgets are concerned, the province of Saskatchewan last year came closer to balancing its budget than did any province west of the maritimes. The province of Ontario did not come within $5,000,000 of balancing its budget, whereas Saskatchewan came within half a million. I do not know

The Address-Mr. Turnbull
what the figures are for this year; I am speaking for last year only. In 1928 the agricultural revenue of the three western provinces was $843,000,000, and in 1932, by reason of circumstances not under the control of the ptrairie governments, that .revenue fell to $273,000,000. Under these circumstances is it fair to say that the troubles in the western provinces are due to reckless extravagance on the part of their administrations? I wish to say to the hon. gentleman through you, Mr. Speaker, that the people of the west have been pretty fair customers of the people of eastern Canada, and the people in the east are beginning to realize that fact. Is it right and proper, then, to jump on your customer when he is down, instead of giving him a hand to help him to get on his feet again and resume a position in which he can buy? For that reason I ask the people of the east, who have had good crops all these years and have received more for their agricultural products than we have, owing to their proximity to a market, to be more charitable in their views of the western people who are doing their best in a time of adversity to play their part as citizens of the country in which they live.

During the visit of the leader of the opposition to western Canada, when he began to appreciate the conditions facing the people there he grew very sympathetic and produced a great number of policies that he bad forgotten about since 1921. I could imagine him as a modern Rip Van Winkle who had gone to sleep in 1921 with a 1919 platform or chart before him. He woke up in 1931 to find the 1919 platform as good as new because it had never been used. The famous chart had not even a pin prick on it. He came into that country under these conditions and told the fanners and other people that he was in favour of a national scheme of unemployment insurance, and further that they ought -to have crop insurance to some extent at least against drought, insects and the other matters beyond the farmers' control. The right hon. gentleman promised these farmers things which he knew, or ought to have known perfectly well, weTe not within the power of himself or any dominion government to grant. Take crop insurance; hail insurance in some parts of that country costs 12 per cent-what would it coat to cover damage by grasshoppers and drought, to say nothing of the other plagues to which farm crops are subject?
Because of these promises I have gone to a little detail in getting the history of unemployment insurance in this country. In the first place, the promise of a national scheme of unemployment insurance was contained in the famous Liberal platform of 1919. Under pressure by the labour members from North Winnipeg and Winnipeg North Centre in 1926 a part of that paragraph that promised old age pensions was implemented by giving

grants in aid to such provinces as desired to enter into the scheme. That is the only part of that paragraph that anything was done with at all. The principle of grants in aid, or the placing of money raised by dominion taxation in the hands of the provinces to be disbursed, was afterwards declared by the leader of the opposition to be a vicious principle, and no further attempt was made to carry that principle into legislation. But pressure came from the third party in the house to do something with regard to these matters; election time was coming on and it was necessary to do something. So in 1928 a motion regarding unemployment insurance was referred to the committee on industrial and international relations for investigation, and report. A report, of the committee as set out in the journals of the house dated May 16, 1928, reads in part as follows:
(1)	That the necessity of a policy providing some method of unemployment insurance is one that will inevitably have to be dealt with before long as a solution in part of the industrial problems of the present day.
That sounded all right. Clause 2 accepted the principle of contributory unemployment insurance. Clause 3 reads:
That the evidence of the justice department makes it clear that the responsibility for such legislation rests on the provincial authorities; it being within their jurisdiction under the provisions of the British North America Act, but that it would be within the power of parliament to contribute by grant to such provinces as adopted such legislation, following the precedent set in the matter by technical education, highway construction and more recently the old age pension act.
But the theory of grants in aid having been declared to be a vicious principle, the report of the committee, although adopted by the house, was not followed up. The committee evidently knew the attitude of the government, because instead of recommending immediate action, they recommended by clause 7 that the matter be again referred to the committee on industrial and international relations at a subsequent year. In 1929 the question was again referred to the same committee, and the committee again endorsed the principle of unemployment insurance on a contributory basis. Clauses 2 and 3 of the report, however, read as follows:

The Address-Mr. Turnbull
(2)	Your committee recognizes that while it is highly desirable that such legislation should be uniform in all the provinces and while social insurance has a federal aspect, nevertheless, according to the Department of Justice, under our constitution legislative jurisdiction in relation to the establishment of a compulsory system of unemployment insurance is vested exclusively in the provincial legislatures.
(3)	Your committee finds that the provinces on being consulted by the Department of Labour with regard to their attitude towards the establishment of a general scheme, do not appear to be prepared to take immediate action.
There the matter was dropped. The committee recommended that the federal government be requested to bring the matter before the next dominion-provincial conference. I am informed that the question of unemployment insurance was one of the items dealt with at such a conference a year or two ago, and that the attitude of the provinces was that they are masters in their own house, so that in spite of all these facts, which are well known to the leader of the opposition, we find him during the summer going out into western Canada and telling the people that he is again favourable to a national system of unemployment insurance as well as crop insurance. Similar language was used by him in all parts of western Canada. That is the sort of remedy offered by him to people who are in misfortune; he knows perfectly well he has no power to carry out his promise but he hopes it may carry him into office at the next election. I submit that the only insurance that the leader of the opposition was interested in was the insurance of a job for himself on this side of the house after the next election; he was more interested in his success in that election than in the welfare of the people of western Canada.
In connection with that very question of unemployment insurance it might be well to remind the house that we have heard a great deal, during the last three or four years, about the number of unemployed in Canada. It is to be noted that figures furnished by the United States government indicate that during the last six years in which our predecessors were in office 436,000 Canadians migrated to the United States. They migrated there to get jobs that they could not get in Canada, even during the years of supposed prosperity under the last government. Had those 436,000 not been admitted to the United States during those six years our hon. friends opposite would have had a real unemployment problem on their hands before 1930. Unemployment did not originate in 1930. Hon. members know that in Saskatchewan 74726-21 i
before the provincial election in 1929, there were parades of unemployed to the Hon. Mr. Gardiner to ask him what he was going to do to take care of the unemployed in Regina. If they will read the press they will also know that the leaders of that parade were arrested the next day, brought before the magistrate, and imprisoned for vagrancy. That was the way they treated the unemployed when they were in office, but they are very nice and kind to them now that they are out.

I would rather leave the speech of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) in that regard to the electors of Saskatchewan. They know what John I. McFarland has done; they know what it has meant to them.

They might have put it in storage but they could not have found a purchaser for it except as the wheat moved for export. In that case the carry-over would have been on the hands of the farmers and the cash would have been in the hands of somebody else, instead of the carry-over being on the hands of somebody else and the cash in the pockets of the farmers.
With regard to the reduction in wheat acreage and with regard to the restriction of production, the minimum amount that we are permitted to sell under the agreement is
200,000,000 bushels. In three years since 1921, and including that year, our sales of wheat and wheat in the form of flour combined have been less than 200,000,000 bushels. In the last year that my hon. friends opposite were in office, the year when they had the advantage of those wide markets of which they have spoken, the year when France and Germany and Italy and Czechoslovakia and all the other countries to which we formerly sold wheat shut out our wheat from their markets in spite of the so called low tariff
The Address-Mr. Turnbull

policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, the total amount of wheat sold by Canada was 155,000,000 bushels. When we get a restriction agreement that permits us to sell 200,000,000 bushels it is said to be terrible, to be restricting the farmers' sales, but when other countries put up their tariffs against us, with no protest from hon. gentlemen opposite, so that we can sell only 155,000,000 bushels, that is friendship for the farming population.
There is one matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens); that is the question of consumption. The average consumption of wheat in Canada and the United States has been rapidly decreasing. Very eminent gentlemen, who are authorities on dietetics and who are supposed to be in the pay of people outside of this country, are persuading people all through Canada and the United States that white bread is not good for them and that they ought to eat something else. I understand they even made an impression on some hon. gentlemen opposite during the vacation. In any event the average consumption of wheat in this country and the United States has been rapidly diminishing. At the present time we are consuming about four and a half bushels of wheat per capita in Canada. There are twelve countries, most of them large buyers of wheat from Canada, whose per capita consumption is greater than ours, and there are nineteen countries whose per capita consumption is less than it is in Canada. If the
130,000,000 people living on the North American continent were to increase their consumption of wheat by one bushel per capita we would have 130,000,000 bushels of this carry-over taken care of at once, and I am told that about one slice of white bread eaten every day will do it.
My suggestion to the Minister of Trade and Commerce is that he get in touch with the national recovery administration in the United States to see whether between the two governments, by an advertising campaign of some kind-a "use more wheat" campaign if you like

you cannot persuade the people of these two countries, as part of the national recovery campaign, to use more bread and in that way assist the agricultural population. Since we have large numbers of United States magazines coming into this country, an advertising campaign carried on by this medium would give cheap advertising in Canada so far as we are concerned.
Having dealt with these matters I wish to touch for a moment or two on the question of national recovery. We are asked from time

to time why we do not do the things that are being done in the United States of America. We are asked why we have not had codes in industry, why we have not set hours in labour, why we have not. set rates of pay and so on. There is a simple answer to all these questions, even if they were good things to do. The simple answer is that the Dominion government has not the legislative authority with which to take any of these steps. It is asked "Why do you not do it under the peace, order and good government clauses?" The peace, order and good government clauses of the British North America Act do not transfer legislative jurisdiction from the various provinces to the dominion at all; they provide for the peace, order and good government of this country within the limits of the jurisdiction of the Dominion government. It is true that in time of war the legislative jurisdiction of the Dominion government is greatly enlarged in order to deal with those matters that are necessary in order to carry a war to a conclusion, but they do not go the extent of allowing the Dominion government, in time of peace, to usurp any of the functions of the provincial governments.
There are those who sneer at the idea that the British North America Act stands in the way of some things that it may be thought desirable to have done. I heard an hon. member say the other day that the British North America Act was used by the party in power as a shield with which to shelter itself from the need for taking action, no matter which party was in power. I have just read the report of the committee of the house, which at that time was under the chairmanship of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), and which, though composed mostly of Liberals, also had represented in its membership Conservatives and gentlemen from the third party in this house. The committee concurred unanimously in the view that unemployment insurance was purely a question of provincial jurisdiction.

The Address-Mr. Turnbull

speechtext: What about old age pensions?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The same was true with regard to old age pensions as a federal scheme. Possibly unemployment insurance can be handled in the same way, provided the provinces are agreeable to having it done in that way and provided we can get away from the idea that it is a vicious principle for the Dominion government to raise money by taxation and allow the provincial governments to spend it. I am somewhat in agreement with the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in that regard. I think the proper way is not to try to get around the constitution but rather to try to amend the constitution. If it should be a matter of federal responsibility let us amend the constitution and make it a federal responsibility, and then we will not need subterfuges in order to attain the desired end.
The question of national recovery is bound up with questions of monetary policy. Perhaps so far as that is concerned the Dominion government has the legislative jurisdiction, but monetary policy is not the only thing to be considered. This country will not be restored to its one time prosperity by monetary policy alone, neither will it be restored just by the setting up of a central bank. There are those who believe that once a central bank is set up everything will be all right, that anyone who wants money will be able to get it in a bundle. One of the leaders of the C.C.F. party in Saskatchewan said that their policy would be to provide all the money desired by those who produced goods as well as all the money desired by those who purchased the goods. But there is more than monetary policy involved; there is the question of distribution and the marketing of goods. That is both an internal and external question; it has to do both with our domestic and foreign markets. The jurisdiction is divided in that case; the Dominion government has control of exports while the provincial governments have control of marketing within their own borders, and that is another item that must be taken into consideration in considering the question of national recovery.
There is also an economic policy to be considered; the control of production, if that is thought to be essential; the regulation of production, if that is thought to be essential, and the establishment of credits, if that is thought to be essential. I am told there are industries in this Dominion of Canada which already have established codes of their own- it may be one of those things that we hear
called combines, but there are combines which, if they conduct themselves in the interests of the public, are very desirable- and such industries in Canada as have established codes of their own. have thereby regulated their own business in such a way that their products are on the markets of Canada at less money than they were when they followed a policy of ruthless competition instead of one under which they regulate production among themselves.
Then there is the question as to what part industrial relationships should play in the national recovery. The question of hours of labour, rates of pay, insurance against ill health, insurance against accident, insurance against unemployment-these are matters which must be dealt with if a general national recovery is to be brought about. There is the matter of social relationships, and the question of pensions, whether they be war pensions, old age pensions or any other kind. All these are matters in connection with which there is divided jurisdiction.
Then, there is the question of taxation which ought to be considered, and that of the dominion raising money by taxes and giving it to the provinces to be spent. There is the question of the field of taxation. Let us for example consider the income tax. As a western member let me state that in the province from which I come there is an income tax for federal purposes, and one for provincial purposes. Both those income taxes bear heavily upon the western members. It costs us money to come to Ottawa to live and to earn our sessional indemnity. While a commercial traveller is allowed his expenses

while away from home, a member of the House of Commons is not allowed those expenses by the federal government. The provinces have followed the lead of the dominion, and the result is that so far as sessional indemnity is concerned members from Saskatchewan are assessed twice on their gross incomes rather than once on their net incomes. So that there is the question of income tax.
The fact of the matter is that the Dominion government is being asked in all parts of Canada to stage a national recovery while the powers essential to such recovery are largely in the hands of provincial legislatures. The position is an impossible one. In the year 1934 the scheme of things in Canada is entirely changed from what it was in 1867. There have been improvements in transportation, improvements in communication, and a closer relationship between the people in different parts of the country, with the result

The Address-Mr. Turnbull
that matters which were formely of local and private concern or interest are now dominionwide in their scope and extent. The scheme which was wise in 1867 and which operated under conditions prevailing in that year and many years since may not be wise to-day. In those days people lived in communities separated from each other; they had their individual problems which did not infringe on the individual problems of others; they could take care of their own difficulties in a local way. But now our country is bound together by business relationships, communications and transportation; things which formerly affected the people of only one province now affect the dominion as a whole. The production of wheat in Saskatchewan, a local and private matter having to do with property and civil rights, is one which profoundly affects the whole dominion. It is a matter with which the Prime Minister of Canada could not deal at the conference in London until he had before him the request of the three prairie provinces so to deal with it. And when any person says, Mr. Speaker, that this wheat agreement arrived at in London is the result of a Tory policy of restriction, let me say to him that it is the result of the combined requests of a Farmer government in Alberta, a Conservative-Farmer government in Saskatchewan, and a Farmer-Liberal government in Manitoba. The Dominion government in carrying out its policy was only carrying out the policy asked for by those three prairie provinces through their representative, Major Mac-Pherson, whose signature is affixed to the wheat agreement.
The question of reduction of acreage, if there is any reduction-I do not believe there will1 be-is a matter for the provinces to handle. Again we are dealing with a question of property and civil rights, a point which the provinces fully realize. There are those who used to say that the Prime Minister of Canada was an economic nationalist. A few years later when we got the imperial treaties these people broadened their views and stated that he was an economic imperialist. In the course of a few more years they may get further wisdom and describe him as he really is. The fact is that only two international conferences in the last ten years have been successful and have resulted in action, the imperial economic conference of 1932, and the wheat conference in London in 1933. Strange to say, the man who is said not to want to have any truck or trade with his neighbours, the man who has been

referred to as an economic nationalist, was chairman of both those conferences.
The necessity for national recovery is apparent to everybody. Before this federal government can bring about national recovery it must have legislative jurisdiction placed in its hands. In 1934 we need more centralized authority than we did in 1867, all of which brings me to the point that a thorough revision of the British North America Act with regard to the respective legislative jurisdictions of the dominion and the provinces is long overdue. The field of legislative jurisdiction and the field of taxation ought to be reexamined in the light of present circumstances. The fullest protection as now provided for in the act should be given to minorities, but with respect to monetary, economic, social and industrial relationships there should be a revision of the whole scheme of affairs so that the central authority should have control over those things which have a bearing upon the welfare of Canada as a whole. I am of the opinion that the sooner we set about making this change the better.
Unfortunately there are some who hold the view that if one province dissents from an amendment to the British North America Act there can be no amendment. I believe the sooner we get away from that idea the better. We must get down to the point where we will think that even with respect to the British iNorth America Act-and I understand fully the contractual argument-we are dealing with more than a matter of contract among the provinces. In the interests of a minority province whose economic welfare depends upon the welfare of the dominion as a whole I submit that the majority should rule, and that the act should be revised and revamped in all its phases touching upon the welfare of the dominion as a whole, regardless of whether or not one or two provinces hold out against such revision.
I wish to congratulate the government upon the improvement which has taken place in Canada in the last eight months. I do not say that the improvement is due entirely to the action of the government, because we know that world conditions affect our country as all others. I congratulate the government because in a time of stress it has stood firmly through adversity, has led the Canadian people on the right path, and, more than that, has kept the Canadian people from straying into by-ways so that when world recovery, assisted by our legislative scheme, is brought about, we may be in a position to play a large part in it. We are making as much progress as any other country in the world. We are increasing our exports and our imports. We

The Address-Mr. Young
are increasing our exports to the empire and our imports from it. To hon. members who say that because we have done that we have prevented ourselves from trading with the rest of the world, let me say that we are increasing our exports to and our imports from the rest of the world. In all phases we are adding to our prosperity. When the day comes that western Canada can produce again a crop of wheat-they will do it again-and when they add to their wheat production the live stock they are producing to-day, it will be surprising how fast the wheels of industry will begin to turn in the east and how fast the people of the west will begin to pay their debts and again take their places among the prosperous provinces of Canada.
