Mr. Speaker, there is only one remark of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Turnbull) to which I wish to direct the attention of the house. He said that in the spring of 1932, when the relief bill was before the house, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) by his opposition to that bill prevented the farmers of western Canada who had been dried out the jmar before and needed seed, from getting their seed for six weeks. My hon. friend is not well informed on that matter.
It will be recalled that in the summer of 1931, when it was first realized that the entire western prairie country was to have no crop and likely no seed in the country next year, the government took the precaution of buying what wheat there was in the country and holding it for distribution amongst the farmers the following spring. In the spring of 1932, when the relief bill was before this house and members on this side were opposing it through a protracted debate, it was freely said from the other side that the farmers of western Canada would not get their seed until that bill passed. I am going to be kinder to the Prime Minister and the government than the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) was, because with all his faults the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was not guilty of doing the thing of which the hon. member accuses him. During that debate I had occasion to go west, and when I arrived the snow was still on the ground, the frost had not yet come out, no work had commenced on the land, but the farmers were drawing their seed home from the elevators, and getting it from the Saskatchewan relief commission, and when I came back I found that the same debate was still going on; and so I say I am kinder to the Prime Minister than was the hon. member for Regina. I do not
accuse him of depriving the farmers of the west of seed grain until the opposition yielded and allowed the bill to pass.
As I listened the other day to the Prime Minister, he gave us figure after figure, tables and columns of figures, to prove that at last we were turning the corner and that prosperity was beginning to dawn upon us, until I began to wonder if it was really so. But afterwards, studying the figures carefully in Hansard, I was not so sure of it. At page 63 of Hansard the Prime Minister gives us four tables comparing conditions in Canada with conditions in other countries. The object of giving us this table was to prove that if conditions are bad here they are at least as bad elsewhere. They tell us that misery loves company, that a person can always find some consolation from contemplating others who are as badly off as himself but that has well been described as the " consolation of the damned." It is true that the rest of the world is in distress, but if that teaches us anything, if we can learn anything from the four tables that appear on page 63 of Hansard, it is that the world is a unit, that if one country suffers we all suffer, that if one country prospers we all prosper. When we hurt one country we hurt all countries. When we strangle trade with one country we strangle our own trade. After studying these tables which the Prime Minister submitted I hope that he will never again stand up on a public platform in this country and boast that he is strangling the trade of the foreigner.
On the next page, 64, the Prime Minister submits a table showing improvement figures based on actual quantities; to prove his statement that conditions were getting better in this country, he gives the figures for February, November and December, all in the same year, and right at the top of the table appear the words "No adjustment for seasonal variations." To prove the country is prosperous the Prime Minister shows that in February of last year we imported six million pounds of raw cotton, in November nineteen million pounds, and in December nearly twenty million pounds. Well, anybody would expect -that our cotton manufacturers would bring in more cotton in the fall, when raw cotton comes on the market, than in February, after the market has been supplied. The Prime Minister does not compare the same months in different years. He compares different months in the same year, and the table is of no value whatever.
But if this table were an indication that trade is improving, it is also an indication
The Address-Mr. Young

that trade has gone the other way. The figures which he submits in most instances show an improvement from February to November, and then a very decided reaction from November to December. Take newsprint production, for instance. The figures show that our production in February was 125,000 tons, in November 193,000 tons, and in December 175,000 tons. Of planks and boards our exports in February were 37,000,000 feet; in November 102,000,000; in December
99.000.	000; copper exports, February 1,326,000 pounds, November 4,498,000, and -then the figure dropped in December to less than
2.000.	000 pounds; nickel exports, February
3.000.	000 pounds, November 8,500,000, and then a drop to 6,500,000 in December; car-loadings, February 133,000, November 201,000, and then a drop to 157,000 in December; bank debits, February 81,830,000,000, November
82.837.000.	000, and then down to $2,491,000,000, in December, or a decline of nearly $350,000,000; contracts awarded, February 83,000,000, November 810,000,000, and then only 88,000,000 for December. So I say that this table which the Prime Minister has submitted as a sign of prosperity is no indication of prosperity because although it shows an improvement from February to November, it also shows a sharp decline from November to December.
On the same page the Prime Minister gives a table showing the wholesale prices of Canadian farm products, indicating that the average price for the year 1932 was 48-4 per cent of what it was in 1926, and that in 1933 it was 51 per cent. But he makes no allowance for the fact that our dollar in the meantime had gone down from 88 cents in gold to 73 cents in gold, and if you make allowance for that difference, then in order to hold our own the average price for 1933 should have been 561 per cent instead of 51 per cent.
Turning over to page 68 of the Prime Minister's speech, there he gives another example of returning prosperity. He says that he knows one merchant in the city of Ottawa who told him that December was the best month he had had in six years for cash business. But that is no indication of anything. It would be strange indeed if somebody was not doing better than others in this depression. What kind of a merchant was this? It might have been a coal dealer for all we know, and anybody who knows the kind of weather we had here in December will realize that a coal dealer would certainly do more business in that month than in the same month in any of the previous six years.

On page 70 the Prime Minister says that our exports in 1933 amounted to 8531,474,000 as compared with $493,808,841 in 1932. Here again he makes no allowance for the changed value of our dollar. Let us bring those figures to a common denominator and measure them by the unvarying yardstick of gold. Our dollar in 1932 was worth 8S cents in gold; that is the average price for the year; its average price for the year 1933 was 73 cents in gold. Therefore in 1932, when our dollar was worth 88 cents in gold, our exports amounted to $434,551,000, and in the next year, 1933, when our dollar was worth 73 cents in gold, our exports really amounted to only $387,000,000, when you take into account the changed value of the dollar, and that is a very decided reduction when measured by the unvarying yardstick of gold.
On the same page of Hansard the Prime Minister says:
But there is something more than that. The principal fall in our external trade has been with the United States of America.
Further on he says, referring to the Americans:
They have raised almost prohibitive tariffs against the world. They have declined to permit other countries to find markets in their country, and they expect to find markets in ours.
In all the years I have been here I have been trying to denounce the tariff policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, but I have never been able to frame a sentence which so clearly and concisely damns the policy of this government. Let us change the pronoun and we will find that it applies with equal truth. Instead of "they," let us put in "we," and it will read this way:
We have raised almost prohibitive tariffs against the world. We have declined to permit other countries to find markets in our country, and we expect to find markets in theirs.
Did any hon. member on this side ever draw up such a damning indictment of the government's policy as that?
While I am speaking on trade with the United States, let me give a few figures. We have been told repeatedly, especially when we were in office, that this country had an adverse trade balance with that country of some $300,000,000 per year, that we were buying that much more from them than they were buying from us. It was then claimed that the right hon. gentleman would put a stop to that when he got into power. The figures given were substantially true. For the two years 1928 and 1929 our total imports from the United States amounted to $1,715,000,000 and our total exports to that country during

The Address-Mr. Young
the same two years amounted to $1,057,000,000, leaving a so-called adverse trade balance of $S5S.030,000 for the two years. Let us look at the figures for our trade with the whole world. During the same two years our exports to the whole world amounted to $2,-
533,000,000 and our imports amounted to $2,513,000,000. That is, our exports and imports to and from the whole world were almost in exact balance, one almost exactly paid for the other. But our exports to the United States were $658,000,000 less than our imports. What did that mean? It meant that while we were buying more from the United States, we were buying less from other countries, and our exports to the whole world were just about paying for our imports. You will recall that 1928 and 1929 were the years when the American people were extending enormous credits to the people of Europe. The people of Europe were using those credits to buy our wheat, our lumber, our newsprint, our surplus manufactured goods and so on. They could not pay for them with their own money, but the Americans had extended credit to them and said: "Go ahead; buy Canadian wheat, buy Canadian lumber, buy Canadian newsprint, buy Canadian mineral products and so on and we will pay for them." And they did. We sold our products to Europe and we received payment from the United States. We received payment in goods-the kind of goods we wanted-and that was the thing that hon. gentlemen opposite complained of; that was the thing they said they would stop. That is the thing that has been stopped. When the people of Europe could not obtain any more credit in the United States, when the United States would no longer pay for the goods that Europe was buying from us, then we could not sell our surplus products. Yet my hon. friends glory in the ruin they have wrought.
Let us now consider the wheat agreement. On page 75 of Hansard the Prime Minister is reported as quoting a telegram which he received from the premiers of the prairie provinces. I shall read only the third paragraph, which is:
That in view of the present large world surplus of wheat and the present prospect of a further large Canadian crop, some plan of curtailment of wheat production in or exports from the four principal exporting countries is essential to any such price increase;
It is upon that telegram that the wheat agreement has been based. The Prime Minister went over to the economic conference and because he had been advised by the provincial premiers that there was a surplus of wheat in the world, that because of that surplus we could not sell our wheat and it was advisable to curtail production, he took part in the proceedings which resulted in the wheat agreement. Since the opening of this session he has been good enough to place in our hands a pamphlet setting forth the reasons why this wheat agreement is necessary. I shall not take the trouble to read from the pamphlet, but I have made a synopsis of the figures which are to be found on page 8. This pamphlet is the strongest case that could be made out in support of the world agreement. It states that during the thirty years, from 1885 to 1915 the world wheat acreage increased by 100,000,000 acres, an average increase of three and one-third million acres per annum, and that world production in the same time increased by
2.000.	000.000 bushels, an average increase of over 66,000,000 bushels per annum. The pamphlet also tells us that that increase was just about enough to take care of the steadily increasing requirements of the world for no surplus had been built up during all those years. From 1915 to 1922 the world wheat acreage decreased by 41,000,000 acres while production decreased by 850,000,000 bushels. In the next ten years, from 1922 to 1932, the world acreage increased by 75,000,000 acres as compared with the 1922 figure, or 34,000,000 acres more than it was in 1915. Had the normal rate of increase continued from 1915 to 1932, the increase would have been
57.000.	000 acres. As it was, the acreage in 1932 was only 34,000,000 acres more than it was in 1915. World production in 1932 had increased 800,000,000 bushels above what it was in 1922, but it must be remembered that in 1922 it was down 850,000,000 bushels. The production in 1932 was 50,000,000 bushels less than in 1915. The production figures are not yet complete for 1933-34, but it is estimated that it will be 175,000,000 bushels less than in 1932. The total production for 1933-34 will be 225,000,000 bushels less than in 1915. Under normal conditions there should have been an increase of 1,250,000,000 bushels in that time, and the world would have been able to take care of it.

What does

speechtext:
It proves that this so-called surplus of wheat is mythical-that there is no surplus. But wheat is not the only food of the human race. People might be eating less wheat and more of something else and production might swing from wheat to rye, from wheat to barley or from wheat to some-
The Address-Mr. Young

thing else. In order to get a true picture we must consider not the question of whether there is too much wheat in the world, but whether there is too much food in the world. I have before me the figures for the world production of wheat, oats, barley, rye and potatoes, the five principal foods of the white races. World production in these five foods for the year 1932 amounted to 15,490,000,000 bushels. The average world production of the same foods for the five years from 1926 to 1930 was 18,498,000,000 bushels. In other words, instead of being up, the world production of food in 1932 had decreased 16 per cent below the average. The figures for 1931 reveal the fact that the production for that year was 20 per cent below the average.
In the light of these figures how can anyone say that there is an over-production of wheat in the world? Last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) stood in his place in the house and told us that the surplus was rapidly disappearing, that the vast quantities of wheat which the farmers of Europe were in the habit of carrying in the stack and which represented a vast invisible supply had disappeared. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was right when he said that the surplus was largely disappearing, and the time that scarcity is going to overtake us is a year closer than it was when that statement was made. I notice that the minister has not been in his seat while this wheat agreement has been under discussion. I do not blame him because I believe that in his heart he knows there is neither a surplus wheat nor an overproduction. A thousand million people in the world are not getting enough to eat. Give each one of them an extra slice of bread three times a day and the so-called surplus will disappear over night. Some day soon the people of the world are going to wake up to the fact that the world is facing a wheat shortage, that we are actually on the verge of famine. Then the people will rise and demand from their governments an explanation as to why they were not allowed to buy the wheat they needed when the people in other countries were willing to sell it; and the people of this country will rise and demand an explanation as to why this government did not allow us to buy the manufactured goods we needed and which the people of Europe were willing to give in exchange for our wheat.
The trouble is not overproduction of wheat. We must seek the cause elsewhere, and it is to be found in the fact that the governments of the world will not allow their people to buy it, and the governments of the countries that have wheat to sell will not allow their

people to accept goods in exchange for it. The solution of the wheat problem is not to curtail acreage but to find some way of breaking down these barriers that prevent wheat from flowing where it is needed and that stop other goods from coming back in payment for it.
In the prairie section of this country we have only one possible source of wealth, namely, our land. Our soil and our climate are preeminently suited to the growing of wheat. In spite of the fact that we are further from seaboard than any other wheat producing country in the world, we have succeeded in growing wheat and putting it on the world market in competition with all countries. We have met with some measure of success growing it. We have demonstrated our ability to make a living at it, but we have not demonstrated our ability to make a living at anything else. Those who tell us to stop growing grain and go in for mixed farming do not know what they are talking about. The country is, as I say, preeminently suited to the growing of wheat and nothing else, and now we are being asked to abandon the one thing that we can do. To what else can we turn? There is nothing else we can make a living at, and because governments in some other countries are trying to force upon their people an uneconomic policy of trying to feed themselves we are asked to abandon the one thing that we can do. Has any one really practical suggestion been offered by anybody who supports this agreement as to how it will be carried out? How will you enforce it? Are you going to go to each individual farmer and tell him to sow so many acres less, leaving the rest of his land to grow weeds? Are you going to compensate the farmer, or are you going to tell him to gQ ahead and grow all the wheat he likes and then refuse to allow him to sell it? And how will you apportion it? Not one practical suggestion has been offered by anyone supporting the agreement as to how it will be carried out. We have an exhibition in Saskatchewan at the present time of the incompetence of governments. The provincial government is sending out one set of officials to advise the farmers to get busy and prepare to fight the grasshopper plague-because we have twenty-two million acres infested with grasshopper eggs-one set of officials, I say, going out telling the people to fight the grasshoppers lest they destroy the crops, and now another set of officials going out advising the farmers to destroy the crops themselves. This is an example of planned economy-planning done by the state.

The Address-Mr. Young
In my opinion there is no way of carrying out the agreement exeept by some form of centralized marketing under government control, and I wonder how many hon. gentlemen opposite are in favour of the centralized marketing of wheat. How many are in favour of the government taking hold and doing all the marketing? Every government in the world during the past several years has been doing its level best to raise the price of wheat. They have raised tariffs, imposed embargoes, granted bounties, enforced milling restrictions -have done everything conceivable to increase the price of wheat. And the net result of all their activities is the lowest price in history. -Can we never learn anything from experience? Surely it is time for the peoples of the world to tell their governments to get out of the way and let wheat prices find their own level.

There are one or two other matters in the speech from the throne to which I would direct the attention of the house. Mention is made of an attempt to provide intermediate or short term credits for agriculture. It seems to me that if we want to provide intermediate or short term or long term or any other sort of credits for agriculture the first thing to do is to make it possible for agriculture to pay its debts. No one will lend money to the farmer to grow crops that will not pay the expense of growing. The money we pay in interest on our debts is not all interest. Part of it is interest on the money borrowed, part of it is the cost of rendering the service and part of it is insurance against loss. The greater the risk the greater the cost of insurance against loss, and if you want to reduce interest rates the first thing to do is to make the loan safe, and that portion which we call interest, which really goes to cover the risk, will disappear. Then it will be easier to get money, and when money is easier to get, when there is more competition in lending, then the cost of the service will come down and interest also will decline. The first and only way to bring down the rate of interest to farmers is to put the farmers in a position to repay the loans they obtain.
Then there is a proposal to try to relieve unemployment by launching an extensive program of public works, and iit is generally believed that this will be paid for by the
printing of new money. I was startled when the announcement appeared in the press that the Prime Minister would adopt that policy. A week later, speaking in Vancouver, he said that they would have to do some serious thinking before they ventured on such a policy. I hope he has done that very serious thinking. The question arises-Can you relieve unemployment by creating public works? Do you not create as much unemployment as you relieve? In the first place, no program of public works that can possibly be launched in this country will reach all the unemployed. Unemployed are to be found in every nook and corner of the country. You cannot create public works everywhere, and if you take men away from their homes and put them to work on public works you place them under the necessity of paying their board in one section of the country and keeping their homes in another place. Their expenses will eat up their wages and there will be nothing left for them to support their families at home. If you pay for the public works by a direct tax on the people, you take the money out of one man's pocket and put it into another man's, and the man out of whose pocket you take it can buy that much less goods; he buys as much less as the other buys more. You cannot solve unemployment by taking money out of one man's pocket and putting it into somebody else's, because in increasing the purchasing power of the one you are reducing the purchasing power of the other. The way to solve unemployment is to create a demand for goods the production of which will give employment to the people. You must increase the purchasing power of the people, but when you collect taxes from one set of people and give them to another set you reduce the purchasing power of the first set of people by a slightly larger amount than you increase the purchasing power of the others. If you issue bonds, borrowing the money, there is a possibility of bringing into circulation some money that might otherwise be lying idle, but in that event you saddle yourself with interest charges. But suppose you do what it is generally expected will be	done-simply	print	new	money?
What do you do then? You simply add water to the soup, you only thin it out. For with the same quantity of goods in the country to be consumed, and a little more money to buy them with, it just takes a little more money to buy them. The man who gets this new money simply buys goods that otherwise would be bought by others. There is a danger too in creating public works that we saddle ourselves with a maintenance cost which we will
The Address-Mr. Young

find it very difficult later on to carry. I know we have to see that no one starves; we cannot allow people to starve in our midst; we cannot allow undue suffering, but the condition in this country to-day is so serious that the work of relief must be done in the cheapest possible way, and our experience in the past has been that the creation of public works is not the cheapest possible way. We know from our experience in the first year that it took $4 from the treasury to put SI into the pocket of the workingman. Perhaps that was an overstatement, for the other $3 did not all go into profits and capital; it went in part to pay wages to those who produced the materials bought. But it has been found everywhere that the creation of public works is the most expensive form of relief you can dispense. Perhaps there are some kinds of public works that would not saddle us with maintenance costs later on, that perhaps might even be revenue producing. We might spend money draining marshlands, making them fit for cultivation, or perhaps improving our forests. We might even try the experiment of reforestation, that would give employment for the time being and perhaps produce revenue later on. There are places where perhaps we could catch the spring run-off of water and hold it against the dry seasons. But speaking broadly the cheapest way to handle the unemployment situation is by paying direct relief, and the finances of this country will not stand relief in any other but the cheapest way.
One other matter, that of the central bank. We are to have a central bank; the Macmillan commission has recommended it; the government is pledged to it, the opposition and the third party all seem disposed to have it Then the question arises: What kind of central bank are we going to have, and how are we going to run it? I think a great many people are due for disappointment when the central bank comes into being. There are those who think that the central bank is going to force the other banks to lend us money whether we are likely to be able to pay it back or not. There are others who say a central bank is one where the government can get all the money it wants without taxing the people. I heard it said that a central bank is one where a municipality can go with its tax roll and deposit the roll and get the cash instead of collecting the taxes. All these fantastic ideas prevail. What we must remember is that after we get our central bank it will not be able to create wealth out of nothing. It will have to be run by ordinary fallible individuals like ourselves, and the problem will be how to find the very best men to run it; men with understanding, men with courage,

men of character. I want to give this piece of advice to the government, that the directors of this bank should be so chosen that neither the government, nor the banks, nor the big financial interests, nor the captains of industry so-called, nor anybody else will be in a position to put undue pressure on them.

The whole drought area of the province of Manitoba is within my constituency as defined by the provincial government, and for the past four years the people in my constituency have been having great difficulty in the payment of their debts, in regard to relief, and in keeping starvation from their doors. They have their problems and the first brunt of them falls upon the municipalities. I have had to make a few trips to Ottawa on behalf of these people, and I have always found the government willing and ready to lend money to the province of Manitoba to help out the people as and when asked for. So far as lending money to the province of Manitoba for the relief of these people is concerned, I say that on that charge this government can be exonerated. At the end of December, by reason of these -advances, there remained payable to this government by the province of Manitoba slightly over $8,000,000, which indicates that this government has drawn no political lines in helping to solve the relief problem. They have tried to keep body and soul together so far as the people are concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the address I desire to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber), both of whom performed in a very creditable manner their duty of trying to convince the members of this house and the people of the country as a whole of their faith in the present administration. I must confess, however, that I differ from them on many of the points on which they expressed opinions. My constituency being composed of ninety-five per cent of Canadians who are descendants of those of French origin, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, and that of the house, I shall continue my remarks in their and my mother tongue.
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, one who peruses the speech from the throne feels baffled by these first lines:
Canada occupies a leading position amongst those countries where the evidence of a return to permanent prosperity is most convincing.
Indeed, sir, as a Canadian, it gives me great pride to note that Canada occupies an enviable place among the nations of the world in connection with the return to prosperity. However, this position is not all that can be expected, especially when we consider that the population of Canada is composed of descendants of hard working and conscientious men, having at heart the progress and development of their country, offsprings of pioneers who opened to civilization our vast native land, comprising the whole northern part of the American continent and which encloses more wealth, proportionately, than any other country in the world, resources which amount to more than $30,000,000,000 or more than $3000 per capita.
I now come to another interesting paragraph of the speech from the throne:
The prices of agricultural products, which have fallen in recent years to the lowest level in history, have shown substantial improvement in the last few months. My government realize, however, that further increases in price levels are necessary to insure success to those engaged in agriculture.
This simply means that His Excellency the Governor General, in the speech dictated to him by the cabinet, states that agriculture, the fundamental industry of Canada, must receive the consideration of the government. In the course of my remarks, I shall endeavour to prove to the house and to all my fellow-
Wf, Willis.J
citizens that the government has been guilty of negligence, towards the farming class.
That is why His Excellency adds:
My government realize, however, that further increases in price levels are necessary to insure success to those engaged in agriculture.
Prices, sir, automatically find their level according to supply and demand. This is a fundamental and recognized fact. However, in order that the law of supply and demand should become effective, one should not, by means of tariff barriers or other impediments, prevent the producer from receiving fair and equitable prices. Tacitly, therefore, His Excellency recognizes that the government has strangled trade and commerce through its tariff barriers, its famous protection policy. This so heralded policy, in the 1930 election, must be discontinued and our tariff placed on a sound basis. I do not advocate free-trade but a reasonable tariff for revenue purposes, hindering neither trade nor industry. Only when these tariff barriers are down as recommended by His Excellency the Governor General, shall we witness the price of farm products increase.
In order to well understand the conditions existing in Canada, one has but to consult our official statistics. We cannot go astray. Certain members have, at times, contended that these statistics are not accurate. Perhaps, there may sometimes be errors, however, on the whole, one can rely on them. As I intend to particularly discuss agriculture, that industry which has had to suffer more than any other in Canada, I shall do so with statistics in hand and my remarks will especially refer to the paragraph of the speech from the throne which advises the government to study the question relating to the prices and sales of farm commodities.
At page 10 of the booklet Canada, 1934, published under the supervision of the Department of Trade and Commerce, we find the following:
While the farmers' difficulties in 1932 were centered around extremely low prices and' while their hopes lay in the bountiful crop production of the year, a different situation existed in 19S3. Summer drought was widespread across Canada, and prolonged in many sections.
I cannot, sir, see how one can reconcile the speeches delivered in the house by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), and a number of members opposite, with this statement issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce and published in the booklet Canada 1934, showing that price levels were down and farmers, who expected a large crop, were disappointed owing to the very dry season. I wish to refer to the statement, in

C.NJR.-Locomotive Engineers and Firemen
1930, of the right hon. Prime Minister when he promised higher price levels for farm products, and, that, if necessary, he would blast the markets in order to facilitate the sale and marketing of their products. On his return from the London Imperial Conference in 1933, the right hon. Prime Minister issued a program, not with the idea of helping the farmers who had suffered losses owing to the drought but one of curtailment of the wheat acreage. I cannot really understand how one can reconcile these two statements. Let us, however, proceed, because there are still other facts to disclose. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) states in this yearly booklet, in the same paragraph which I quoted a few moments ago:
The increase in prices of farm commodities helped considerably to offset the lower production.
Let us examine what is this increase in the prices of farm commodities mentioned and how it came about, if it ever did. Let us examine closely whether such are the facts, by consulting the bureau of statistics.
In the booklet Canada 1934, at page 47, we find that in 1930, the net returns of agricultural products amounted to $758,000,000, in round figures; in 1934, $538,000,000, and in 1932, $428,000,000. It is quite an easy matter to compare the figures for these various years.
Let us now examine what is the decrease in our agricultural resources. At page 67 of the same publication, we find that in 1931, the agricultural wealth of the country amounted to $5,697,000,000, and in 1932. to $5,070,000,000, namely a difference of $627,000,000 in our agricultural assets. Do the Canadian farmers realize that, according to these official figures, their loss amounts to $627,000,000? There has, therefore, not been any increase, on the contrary, statistics prove there has been a decrease.
In order to clearly show the situation of our industrial activities, I shall quote the Bureau of Statistics in connection with our various industries, including agriculture. In 1930, the value of our industrial products amounted to $3,216,000,000; in 1931, to $2,500,000,000, a difference of $716,000,000. Is that an increase, I ask these gentlemen? It would be very hard to convince me of the fact, when the government figures themselves show a considerable decrease.
There is a spread in manufactured products of more than $300,000,000 in less than, a year. Is that the realization of the pledges made at the election in 1930, so as to capture both the confidence and vote of the Canadian people?
Still referring to the Dominion statistics, I find the following at page 12 of the same 74726-22 J
publication under the heading of price commodities:
In March, 1933 (after three years), wholesale prices began the first appreciable advance that has occurred since 1929. It came after an almost unbroken decline of 42 months during which time the Dominion Bureau of Statistics' general index number of wholesale prices fell by roughly 30 per cent.
That is word for word, sir; it is taken from Canada 1934.
It adds:
Prices in some commodity groups such as farm products had dropped more than double this amount-
Namely 60 per cent.

while manufactured goods showed decreases of less than 20 per cent in many eases.
Much could be said, sir, in connection with the serious results which might be the outcome of this abnormal situation, this discrepancy in the price levels of Canadian farm products and those of manufactured goods.
